documents: The study utilized a handheld device called the iTremor ONE, provided by Head Diagnostics, to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) non-invasively using safe laser technology in a duration of three seconds.
The research was supported by a collaborative PhD studentship between Northumbria University and Head Diagnostics, as well as grants from the Parkinson's Foundation (PF-FBS-1898, PF-CRA-2073).
The study utilized the hand-held device iTremor ONE to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) non-invasively in 33 people with Parkinson's Disease and 31 age-matched healthy controls.
For analytical validation, 22 people with Parkinson's Disease completed a test-retest reliability assessment of OMT measurement, which was assessed using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC).

For clinical validation, 24 people with Parkinson's Disease were tested in 'OFF' (12-hour withdrawal) and 'ON' states of anti-Parkinson's dopaminergic medication to compare OMT response to the intervention.
The study notes that video-based eye-tracking systems lack the sensitivity required to detect ocular microtremor (OMT), which limits the generalisability and interpretation of underlying deficits.
Existing invasive methods for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT), such as the piezoelectric strain gauge technique, require the eyes to be anaesthetised and possess high interobserver variability.

The piezoelectric strain gauge technique for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT) requires a highly trained operator, causes discomfort and eye dryness, and relies on constant uninterrupted contact with the sclera for up to 60 minutes.
The piezoelectric strain gauge technique for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT) has an unknown loading effect of the probe, which makes validation of new techniques against this method undesirable.

The study utilized the iTremor ONE device (Head Diagnostics Ltd., Dublin, Ireland), which employs laser technology to measure Oculomotor Tremor (OMT) with a high-resolution, non-invasive, compact, and portable technique.

The analytical validation component of the study aimed to investigate the test-retest reliability of the iTremor ONE in measuring Oculomotor Tremor (OMT) frequency in Hertz (Hz) in people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD).
The study also investigated the feasibility of measuring Oculomotor Tremor (OMT) using hand-held technology in a real-world clinical setting with people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD).

The study design compared OMT frequency in PwPD against age-matched healthy controls, explored relationships between OMT and disease severity, and examined the effect of dopaminergic medication on OMT.
The full study protocol was published previously at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0313452.

The trial was registered with Clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06051877 and received NHS Research Ethics Committee approval (REF: 23/WM/0004) and an MHRA letter of no objection (REF: CI/2023/0031/GB).

PD participants were recruited from the Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust movement disorders clinic and local PD support groups, with inclusion requiring a diagnosis of PD according to UK brain bank criteria.
Age-matched healthy controls were recruited from family members of PwPD and Northumbria University staff, with a minimum age requirement of 50 years old.

Participants were excluded if they had psychiatric co-morbidity, a history or evidence of head injury, ocular disease such as cataracts, or a clinical diagnosis of dementia or severe cognitive impairment measured by a MoCA score of less than 21.
The study used a single iTremor ONE device operated by the same trained operator for every measurement to ensure consistency.
Clinical validation involved 33 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and 31 healthy controls (HCs), with 22 PwPD assessed in the home environment and 11 PwPD assessed in the laboratory.

Participants were seated in a high-backed chair looking straight ahead at a target at eye level, with room lighting controlled consistently and testing conducted in a quiet environment free from noise and interruption.
Three ocular motor tremor (OMT) readings per eye were averaged for each participant.

To assess the effect of levodopa, 24 PwPD fasted from dopaminergic medication for a minimum of 12 hours prior to the 'OFF' state assessment, then took their morning dose and waited 60 minutes before the 'ON' state assessment.
Data was analyzed using SPSS version 28 (IBM Inc, IL, USA), with normal data distribution confirmed using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and Shapiro-Wilk tests.
The study did not control for multiple comparison corrections (e.g., Bonferroni) due to its exploratory nature, which may bias the results by increasing the risk of Type I errors.
Where valid OMT readings could not be obtained, the data were treated as missing and excluded from analysis using available case analysis.
Known groups validity was examined using an ANOVA with group (PwPD vs. HCs) as a between-subject factor, followed by Tukey post-hoc analysis to determine individual group differences.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis tested the performance of OMT frequency from each eye in discriminating PwPD from HCs, with the optimal cut-off point determined as the point closest to the corner (0,1) with a false positive rate of 0% and sensitivity of 100%.
The study used paired t-tests to compare OMT measurements between 'ON' and 'OFF' medication states in Parkinson's disease participants.
The analytical validation cohort included 22 participants with Parkinson's disease who had mild to moderate disease severity and a mean MoCA score of approximately 27.

The clinical validation cohort included 33 participants with Parkinson's disease and 31 healthy controls, with the Parkinson's disease group age-matched to the control group and having a mean MoCA score of approximately 27.

The response to known intervention cohort included 24 participants with Parkinson's disease who had a mean MoCA score of approximately 27 when 'OFF' medication and approximately 26 when 'ON' medication.
Test-retest reliability for OMT frequency was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), which were all greater than 0.90, indicating excellent agreement between home visit readings.

The mean difference between first and second visit OMT readings was 1.14 Hz for the right eye, 1.70 Hz for the left eye, and 1.73 Hz for both eyes, with limits of agreement of 6.6%, 7.4%, and 7.5% respectively.

OMT measurements were repeated by the examiner when the iTremor ONE device reported inability to take a reading due to circumstances such as eye blinks, obstruction from eyelashes or lids, or changes in gaze direction.
The study compared OMT measurements between a group of 33 participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and a group of 31 healthy controls (HC).
The PwPD group consisted of 19 males and 14 females with a mean age of 69.06 years (SD 7.56), a mean disease duration of 5.08 years (SD 3.75), and a mean UPDRS III score of 35.94 (SD 17.71).
The HC group consisted of 12 males and 19 females with a mean age of 67.32 years (SD 9.92) and a mean education level of 16.01 years (SD 4.34).

A subgroup analysis of 24 PwPD participants was conducted comparing OMT measures during the OFF medication state (mean hours since L-dopa 1.41, SD 0.88) and the ON medication state (mean hours since L-dopa 15.00, SD 3.75).

Reliability of the OMT measurements was assessed using Intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) calculated between Visit 1 and Visit 2, yielding values of 0.94 (95% CI 0.86-0.98) for the right eye, 0.93 (95% CI 0.82-0.97) for the left eye, and 0.92 (95% CI 0.81-0.967) for both eyes.
Diagnostic value of OMT assessment for PwPD was evaluated using ROC curve analysis and Area Under the Curve (AUC) calculations, which resulted in an AUC range of 0.745 to 0.773.

Convergent validity was assessed by correlating OMT frequency with age, sex, disease duration, and overall UPDRS motor score, as well as specific MDS-UPDRS motor subsection items such as speech (item 3.1).

The study compared ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency between people with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD) and healthy controls (HC), utilizing clinical measures including the MDS Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale III (UPDRS), Hohen & Yahr Stage (H&Y), Falls Efficacy Scale - International (FES-I), and new Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (nFOGQ).

The analysis of OMT frequency differentiation between PwPD and HCs reported Area Under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.745 for the right eye, 0.773 for the left eye, and 0.760 for both eyes, with corresponding cut-off frequencies of 68.58 Hz, 65.50 Hz, and 65.13 Hz respectively.

The study examined correlations between average OMT frequency and clinical variables such as age, sex, disease duration, UPDRS, H&Y stage, FES-I, nFOGQ, and Levodopa Equivalent Daily Dose (LEDD) for both PwPD and HC groups.
The study utilized the novel iTremor ONE technology to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) in people with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD).
The iTremor ONE device employs a laser-speckle technique for OMT detection, which the authors suggest may offer greater accuracy than previously employed OMT detection techniques.
The analytical validation of the iTremor ONE OMT frequency measurement demonstrated excellent agreement with an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) greater than 0.9.
The study design included a comparison of OMT readings when participants were 'OFF' versus 'ON' anti-Parkinson's medication to assess the response to a known intervention.

The study cohort consisted of a homogeneous group of mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease patients (H&Y stage II-III) without stratification by PD phenotype or disease duration, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other disease stages, subtypes, or comorbidities.
The study was conducted in the North East of England, a geographic limitation that may restrict the generalizability of the results to more diverse populations.
Key confounding factors such as caffeine intake, sleep quality, and home environment were not formally recorded, leaving the potential for unmeasured confounding unexcluded.
The data analyses were limited to univariate correlational and group comparison approaches, rather than multivariable modelling, which may not adequately account for potential confounding variables.

The study used the iTremor ONE device to measure OMT, which may be more accurate than previous piezoelectric tools, resulting in OMT frequency ranges of ~63-70Hz that are lower than the ~68-88Hz reported in a previous study using piezoelectric methods.
The study did not control for day-to-day fluctuations in hours of sleep, stress, and caffeine intake, which were identified as potential sources of variance in OMT frequency measurements.

Participants in the study experienced a learned effect due to familiarisation with the researcher, device, and protocol, which may have contributed to subtle non-significant differences in OMT frequency between the first and second assessments.

The study reported no adverse events and no participant withdrawals, with only minor factors such as blinking, eye movement, and eyelid or lash blocking impacting the ability to obtain OMT measurements.
The study utilized repeated measurements within a session to ensure no data loss occurred despite minor factors like blinking or eye movement that impacted the ability to obtain OMT measurements.
The study measured OMT frequency in participants with Parkinson's disease and healthy older adults, with recorded frequencies ranging from approximately 63 Hz to 70 Hz.

The study assessed the effect of anti-Parkinson's medication on OMT frequency by comparing measurements taken 'OFF' medication (using a 12-hour washout period) against measurements taken 'ON' medication (1 hour after consumption).

The study utilized the UPDRS-III and Hoehn & Yahr (H&Y) scales to assess overall disease severity, noting that these scales rely on expert clinical judgement and focus on specific motor symptoms such as tremor, bradykinesia, and balance.

A previous study referenced in the text categorized participants with Parkinson's disease into 'ON' or 'OFF' medication groups based on the bradykinesia section of the Webster Scale rather than a medication washout period, a method described as subjective and reflective of disease severity rather than medication effect.

The present study used a standard 12-hour washout period for medication withdrawal, whereas a previous study used a longer washout period due to an ongoing medical investigation, with the authors noting that longer washout periods present challenges regarding patient safety and falls risk.

The statistical validity of the results is compromised by the use of a single timepoint baseline and a single group, which necessitates paired tests with small sample sizes that produce wide confidence intervals overlapping zero, rendering reported p-values uninterpretable without control groups or multiple comparison corrections.
The study is a randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate the effectiveness of body weight-supported treadmill training on gait performance in individuals with Parkinson's disease.

Forty patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=20) receiving gait training with a lower-body positive pressure treadmill, or to a control group (n=20) undergoing conventional physiotherapy.
Both the experimental group and the control group trained twice weekly for 4 months.

Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), and classified as primary (gait speed, step length, balance, postural stability) or secondary (quality of life, fear of falling, anxiety).

The study was designed as an exploratory pilot randomized controlled trial without an a priori sample size calculation, enrolling 40 patients with Parkinson's Disease (UPDRS score ≤ 81) from the Parkinson's Outpatient Clinic at IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino-Pulejo" in Messina, Italy, between May 2021 and March 2023. Randomization was performed in a 1:1 ratio using a computer-generated simple random sequence from random.org, with no stratification or block randomization procedures applied.

Participants were included if they had a diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease according to the Movement Disorder Society Clinical Diagnostic Criteria, evidence of Freezing of Gait, age between 50 and 85 years, Hoehn and Yahr stage II to III, and a Mini Mental State Examination score of 24 or higher after age and education correction. Exclusion criteria included the presence of a pacemaker or infusion systems, comorbidities contraindicating physical exercise, and severe visual or auditory impairment.

Blinding of patients and therapists was not feasible due to the nature of the intervention, but all outcome assessments were conducted by evaluators who were blinded to group allocation to minimize detection bias. The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino Pulejo" under protocol U224/22, and participants provided signed informed consent.
The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino Pulejo" (U224/22), and participants provided signed informed consent.
Forty patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to an experimental group (n=20) or a control group (n=20), with no losses to follow-up or discontinuations occurring.

Each participant underwent 20 sessions of gait training twice a week for 4 months, with each session lasting approximately 60 minutes and comprising a 15-minute warm-up, treadmill training, and a 15-minute cooldown.
The experimental group underwent gait training using the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA) with a 60% body weight reduction applied during each session.
Both the experimental and control groups walked barefoot on a treadmill set to a zero-degree incline, with initial speeds based on baseline gait analysis and gradually increased over 20 sessions.

The experimental group underwent gait training using the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA), which utilizes lower-body positive pressure technology to provide body weight support adjustable from 20% to 100% of body weight in 1% increments.

Postural stability was evaluated using the Zebris Medical GmbH pressure-sensitive platform, recording parameters including Center of Pressure (CoP) length, average velocity, 95% confidence ellipse, and load distribution while patients stood still with eyes open and closed for 10 seconds.

Gait parameters were analyzed at T0 and T1 using the BTS Gaitlab system, which is equipped with motion capture systems, force platforms, and electromyographic sensors, following the DAVIS protocol with reflective markers and EMG sensors.

The study enrolled a total of 40 participants, divided into an experimental group of 20 subjects and a control group of 20 subjects. The experimental group had a mean age of 68.5 ± 7.75 years and a mean disease duration of 9 ± 8.5 years, while the control group had a mean age of 65.9 ± 6.73 years and a mean disease duration of 12.5 ± 7.5 years.
Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 with a 5% alpha error, and the authors noted that p-values must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and multiple endpoints.
Primary motor outcomes were presented as means ± standard deviations for normally distributed variables and medians (first and third quartiles) for non-normally distributed variables.

Quantitative gait analysis was performed at baseline (T0) and after treatment (T1) using the BTS Gait Lab system, which includes infrared cameras, force plates, and wireless electromyographic sensors.

Data acquisition followed the DAVIS multifactorial protocol, which combines kinematic, kinetic, and electromyographic assessments using reflective markers placed on standard anatomical landmarks and surface EMG electrodes applied to major lower-limb muscles.
Each participant performed standing and walking trials at a self-selected comfortable speed during the gait analysis sessions.

The Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I) is a 16-item questionnaire with scores ranging from 16 to 64, used to measure fear of falling based on low perceived self-efficacy in avoiding falls during daily activities.

The Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39) consists of 39 items grouped into eight domains, where each item is scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 0 to 4 and domain scores are transformed into a 0 to 100 scale indicating negative impact on quality of life.

The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) consists of 14 items, each scored on a 5-point scale from 0 to 4, resulting in a total score range of 0 to 56 where higher scores indicate greater anxiety severity.

The study applied surface EMG electrodes to major lower-limb muscles and extracted outcomes including hip, knee, ankle, and pelvic joint angles; joint moments and powers; activation timing of tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, quadriceps, and hamstrings; and spatiotemporal parameters such as cadence, step width, step length, stance and swing phases, and gait speed.
The study calculated the Gait Deviation Index (GDI) and Gait Profile Score (GPS) as indices of gait quality to evaluate motor performance changes following the intervention.

The study assessed the normality of continuous data using the Shapiro-Wilk test and analyzed normally distributed data with parametric tests and non-normally distributed data with non-parametric tests applied to raw data.
The study used the unpaired Student's t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for inter-group analysis and the paired Student's t-test or Wilcoxon signed rank test for intra-group analysis.
The study did not analyze raw change scores (Δ = T1 - T0) because these metrics are known to inflate error variance in small samples and were not aligned with the primary objective of the study.
The study calculated Spearman's rank correlation using the change score (Δ) to explore potential associations between quality of life, gait analysis scores, and motor scale.
The study performed statistical analyses using the open source R software package version 4.2.2 with a 95% confidence level and a 5% alpha error, setting statistical significance at p < 0.05.
The study noted that p-values must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and multiple endpoints.
The study utilized a paired Student's t-test for parametric data and the Wilcoxon signed rank test for nonparametric data to analyze intra-group changes from baseline (T0) to post-intervention (T1).
The Mann-Whitney U test was applied as a nonparametric test for inter-group comparisons in the study design.

The experimental group demonstrated significant intra-group improvements in EQ5-D (p=0.03), 10-MWT time (p=0.01), TUG Right and Left (p=0.003), BBS (p=0.001), and 6-MWT (p=0.0003) from baseline to post-intervention.

Gait and locomotion parameters in the experimental group showed significant increases in TS-B (p=0.03), TS-G (p=0.02), Average Gait speed (p=0.02), Step Length Right (p=0.001), and Step Length Left (p=0.004).
Postural stability metrics in the experimental group improved with significant decreases in Ellipse (p=0.04) and Path length CoP (p=0.04) from baseline to post-intervention.
The control group did not exhibit significant improvements between baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), supporting the attribution of experimental group changes to the intervention.
The study design was an exploratory pilot trial, which the authors note limits the feasibility of certain statistical tests and necessitates larger randomized controlled trials for confirmation.

The study utilized a Spearman's rank correlation matrix to analyze the relationship between clinical outcomes and gait/balance parameters, with significance levels defined as p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.

The study utilized a sample size of n=20 per group, a methodological constraint that limits the generalizability of the results. The exploratory nature of the trial increases the risk of Type I error, and a repeated-measures analysis was not feasible despite the assessment of multiple endpoints.

Secondary outcomes were analyzed using paired Student's t-tests for parametric variables, Wilcoxon signed rank tests for nonparametric variables, and Mann-Whitney U tests, with data presented as means ± standard deviations for normally distributed variables and medians with first and third quartiles for non-normally distributed variables.

The study design lacks a control group, which is a fundamental flaw that prevents the isolation of the OMT frequency physiological signal from baseline noise. This absence of a comparator means the reported reliability of the iTremor ONE device cannot be empirically distinguished from consistent sensor jitter or subtle drift, rendering the claim of a distinct signal purely hypothetical.

Replicating the reported OMT frequency variance requires the exact code and parameter settings for the preprocessing pipeline, specifically the cleaning steps applied to the raw video data. Because these scripts are currently absent from the publication, the methodological choices regarding data cleaning remain unverifiable, preventing confirmation that the 1.13 to 1.72 Hz metric is not an artifact of the specific, undisclosed processing parameters.

The study was a retrospective cohort study designed to evaluate the risk of Parkinson's disease associated with schizophrenia and the influence of antipsychotic medications prescribed at the time of schizophrenia diagnosis on Parkinson's disease development.

The study utilized competing risk analysis and Cox regression to analyze the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease, specifically accounting for antipsychotic medication exposure and comorbid conditions.

Researchers accessed the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) data through the NHIS Data Sharing Service website, with access granted only for a predefined period approved for each research project.

The study was a retrospective cohort design utilizing a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea. The dataset included patients diagnosed with schizophrenia and matched controls.

The researchers performed propensity score matching and adjusted for demographic, clinical, and comorbidity variables. Competing risk analysis and Cox regression were used to analyze the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease, considering antipsychotic medication exposure and comorbid conditions.

The de-identified claims data used in the study were obtained from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of Korea and are not publicly available due to NHIS data protection regulations and internal data-use policies.

The study was a retrospective cohort study using a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea covering the period from 2010 to 2021, with data accessed on July 11, 2022.

Schizophrenia was defined by the ICD-10 code F2* requiring one inpatient record or two outpatient records within one year, and patients diagnosed with schizophrenia in 2010 or under 18 years of age were excluded to identify incident new cases.

Patients with schizophrenia were matched with patients without schizophrenia using propensity score matching in a 1:2 ratio based on the Charlson Comorbidity Index score, age, gender, and index year, with the Charlson Comorbidity Index calculated from records one year prior to the index date.
The propensity score matching used a caliper width of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score, with a standardized mean difference of ≥ 0.1 indicating imbalance.
The study defined the outcome of incident Parkinson's disease as a new diagnosis using ICD-10 code G20 occurring at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis.
To minimize diagnostic errors, Parkinson's disease was defined as at least one inpatient diagnosis or two outpatient diagnoses with the G20 code within a one-year period.
The study used Cox regression analysis to calculate crude and adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals for Parkinson's disease incidence rates.
Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, with significance determined by the log-rank test.
Fine-Gray's competing risk analysis was used to determine the risk of Parkinson's disease, considering death as a competing risk factor.
Sensitivity analysis was conducted using time windows of 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date to account for limited knowledge about the onset of Parkinson's disease in schizophrenia patients.
Covariates for the study were based on records from one year prior to the outcome.
The study matched 42,522 patients with schizophrenia to 85,041 controls based on age, gender, matching-period Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, and index year.

All statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA), with a two-sided confidence interval of 0.05 considered to indicate statistical significance.
Sensitivity analysis was conducted using 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date to account for limited knowledge about the onset of Parkinson's disease in schizophrenia patients.

The study utilized de-identified secondary data provided by the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS), and all analyses were conducted within the NHIS-controlled secure research environment with restricted access to ensure data security and privacy.
The study employed Cox proportional regression and Fine-Gray competing risk analysis to calculate crude and adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's disease.

The multivariate analysis adjusted for variables including sex, age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and specific comorbidities such as organic mental disorders, mood disorders, and neurotic stress-related disorders.

The analysis included medication variables for N05A (Antipsychotics), N05B (Anxiolytics), N05C (Hypnotics and sedatives), N06A (Antidepressants), N06B (Psychostimulants for ADHD), and N06D (Anti-dementia drugs).

The study design involved matching patients with schizophrenia against control patients, with 53% of patients in each group scoring three or more points on the matching-period Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI).

To ensure the reliability of the multivariable analysis, the researchers excluded variables with a phi coefficient of 0.4 or higher, specifically the CCI score, medications N05A-N06D, mood (affective) disorders, and hyperlipidemia.

In cases of high collinearity between two diseases, the disease with more associations with other variables was excluded, while in cases of collinearity between a disease and a medication, the medication was excluded.
The study utilized competing risk analysis to evaluate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease risk after adjusting for remaining factors.

The study included 85,041 control participants and 42,522 patients with schizophrenia, with a mean age of 66.36 ± 18.27 years for controls and 66.26 ± 18.48 years for patients with schizophrenia. The mean index year for both groups was 2016.2, and the mean follow-up duration was 4.03 ± 2.98 years for controls and 2.85 ± 2.77 years for patients with schizophrenia.

The study utilized a sensitivity analysis that included competing risk analysis to evaluate the hazard ratio for Parkinson's disease across 1-, 2-, and 3-year periods of comorbidities. A Kaplan-Meier plot was used to assess Parkinson's disease-free survival rates, with a log-rank test yielding a P-value of <0.0001 for the comparison between patients with schizophrenia and controls over a 10-year follow-up period.

The multivariate analysis identified the use of antipsychotic drugs (ATC code N05A) as significantly associated with the development of Parkinson's disease, with a hazard ratio of 1.076 (95% CI: 1.023-1.132, p=0.0045). Neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders were the comorbidities with the highest association with Parkinson's disease development, showing a hazard ratio of 1.380 (95% CI: 1.333-1.429, p<0.001).
The study utilized a large retrospective cohort from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database in South Korea to investigate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.
The study employed both a no competing risk model and a Fine-Gray competing risk model for the sensitivity analysis of Parkinson's disease risk by exposure duration.
Variables with a Phi correlation coefficient greater than 0.4 were excluded from the adjusted hazard ratio analysis.
The study performed a Kaplan-Meier analysis to evaluate the PD-free survival differences between quetiapine users, risperidone users, and non-users.
The study utilized Kaplan-Meier plots to analyze event-free survival for Parkinson's Disease, stratified by schizophrenia status and antipsychotic drug prescription.

Adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's Disease were calculated for patients prescribed antipsychotic drugs, controlling for variables including age, sex, and specific comorbidities such as organic mental disorders and cerebrovascular disease.
The study performed a Kaplan-Meier analysis of event-free survival in Parkinson's Disease specifically stratified by antipsychotic drug prescription.

Adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's Disease were calculated for patients prescribed quetiapine or risperidone, with the analysis adjusting for age, sex, and a list of comorbidities including neurotic disorders and head injury.

The study employed a retrospective observational design using a large-scale administrative claims database, which limits causal inference and restricts access to granular clinical information such as disease severity, symptom onset timing, and neuroimaging results like DaTscan.

To improve diagnostic accuracy and address potential misclassification based on administrative codes, the study defined diseases as requiring at least one inpatient record or two outpatient records within a year.

The analytical framework of the large-scale administrative database made it challenging to reflect individual daily dosing ranges or the exact cumulative duration of exposure, limiting pharmacological interpretation of medication-PD risk associations.

The study focused its analysis on drugs with larger sample sizes and did not perform individual analyses for all medications, while also noting that multiple comparisons across different antipsychotic agents were not explicitly adjusted, which may increase the risk of Type I error.

The researchers addressed potential confounding by incorporating a wide range of clinical and demographic covariates into multivariate models and applied an intent-to-treat approach to mitigate the limitation of being unable to directly assess medication adherence.

To account for the potential impact of premature death before Parkinson's disease onset, the study conducted a competing risk analysis, with results consistent with the standard analysis without competing risks.
The study utilized a cohort design with competing risk adjustment and included a wide range of covariates to specifically focus on schizophrenia patients.
The study performed a focused comparison of two antipsychotic medications to explore their differential impacts on Parkinson's disease risk.
The study evaluated the association of schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease using a large claims data including the majority of the Korean population.
The study applied an intent-to-treat approach to mitigate the limitation of not being able to directly assess medication adherence.
Collinearity analysis was conducted to reduce confounding effects by excluding highly correlated variables in the multivariate models.

The study could not fully account for time-varying treatment patterns, such as medication switching or the use of anticholinergics, which may lead to misclassifying persistent medication-induced symptoms as incident Parkinson's disease.
A 1-year lag period was used in the study, though the risk of reverse causation remains due to Parkinson's disease's long prodromal phase.

The study design lacks a healthy control group, which prevents the isolation of the reported 'distinct physiological signal' from potential artifacts generated by the rigid, single-operator testing protocol.

The reported physiological variance is uninterpretable because the study did not document the specific filtering and motion correction parameters used in the preprocessing pipeline, nor did it provide a healthy baseline for comparison.

The acquisition protocol and reliability statistics were provided without software versions, calibration logs, or code, and the exact preprocessing pipeline and parameter settings required to clean the raw data are missing, rendering the reported variance impossible to verify.

The claim that the measurement represents a novel biological signal is methodologically invalid because the absence of a healthy control group means the observed variance cannot be distinguished from consistent environmental noise or testing artifacts.

The uncorrected p-values constitute a statistical red flag, but the fatal methodological flaw is the missing healthy control group, which prevents the exclusion of the hypothesis that the 'signal' is merely a consistent artifact of the testing environment.
The gait study's reported AUC is unverifiable because the specific preprocessing code and software versions required to check if the signal is an artifact of the cleaning pipeline were not provided.
The missing acquisition parameters and undocumented preprocessing pipeline are the root methodological causes preventing meaningful statistical interpretation of the gait study's small sample size.

The study design lacks a healthy comparator group, which prevents the distinction between a biological marker and a consistent artifact of the testing rig, rendering the central finding an uncontextualized metric.

The tremor measurement study relies on a 31-person healthy control group and an undocumented preprocessing pipeline, which renders its baseline tremor reliability metrics suspect due to missing acquisition parameters.

The rehabilitation intervention trial utilizes a randomized design but lacks a pre-registered analysis plan for its primary endpoint, which complicates the interpretation of the effect size for anti-gravity treadmill gait training.
Independent replication of the medication safety risk estimates is impossible without access to raw diagnostic metadata because the study depends on unadjusted administrative codes.

The cohort study relies on unadjusted diagnostic codes for its administrative data linkage, a methodological choice that introduces significant misclassification bias despite the robustness of the data linkage itself.
Reproducing the rehabilitation paper is currently blocked by the absence of the specific treadmill calibration code, which is required to verify the force plate readings used in the analysis.

The validation study's methods section fails to specify the motion correction algorithms and filter bands used, rendering the specific signal processing choices that could bias the 0.77 AUC result opaque.

The current digital biomarker pipeline is retrospective and opaque, failing to specify exact motion correction and filtering steps, which prevents verification that the observed signal is biological rather than a byproduct of specific preprocessing choices.

The 0.77 AUC for OMT frequency is derived from data that does not distinguish true disease signals from experimental noise or baseline variation, meaning the metric currently lacks the statistical robustness and validated control groups necessary to confirm it as a reliable physiological marker.

The proposed prospective trial must include a healthy control cohort to establish baseline variance, as the current study designs leave researchers blind to what constitutes normal biological noise versus disease pathology.

The existing papers fail to provide independent variance estimates and suffer from uncorrected multiple comparisons, which inflates the Type I error rate and makes cross-validation of the digital biomarker results impossible.
To isolate the signal from noise in the digital biomarker data, a prospective study requires a sample size of at least n = 100 per group to narrow the 95% confidence interval on the effect size.

documents: Ocular microtremor (OMT) oscillates at 70-150 times per second in healthy subjects. Existing invasive measurement techniques, such as piezoelectric strain gauges, require eyes to be held open for up to 60 minutes at a time.
The global prevalence of Parkinson's disease (PD) is estimated at 8.5 million.
The iTremor ONE device uses laser technology to measure ocular motor tremor (OMT) with high resolution in a non-invasive, compact, and portable manner.
The pilot study aimed to investigate the test-retest reliability of the iTremor ONE in measuring OMT frequency (Hz) in people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD).
The study included 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease and 31 age-matched healthy controls, with 22 participants with Parkinson's Disease completing a test-retest reliability assessment.

Test-retest reliability for ocular microtremor frequency measurement in participants with Parkinson's Disease was assessed using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC), yielding a value greater than 0.9.
Mean ocular microtremor frequency was significantly lower in participants with Parkinson's Disease (63.78 ± 4.82 Hz) compared to healthy controls (69.44 ± 6.47 Hz), with a p-value of less than 0.001.

The discriminative ability of ocular microtremor frequency for distinguishing between participants with Parkinson's Disease and healthy controls was reported with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) range of 0.75 to 0.77.

A comparison of ocular microtremor frequency between 24 participants with Parkinson's Disease in 'OFF' (12-hour withdrawal) and 'ON' dopaminergic medication states revealed no significant differences.

The analytical validation of OMT measurement in Parkinson's disease participants included a sample size of 22 individuals who underwent two home-based test-retest assessments performed exactly one week apart.

Disease severity for the 22 Parkinson's disease participants was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's disease Rating scale part III (UPDRS-III) in the "ON" state, defined as 1 hour following Levodopa medication intake.

The OMT measurement protocol required participants to sit in a high-backed chair with dimmed light, remove glasses or contact lenses, and maintain a relaxed gaze at a wall target for approximately 3 seconds per recording.

The OMT measurement procedure involved taking three readings for each eye that were averaged, with the same operator and single iTremor ONE device used for every measurement to control for inter-operator variability.
Clinical validation included a sample of 33 people with Parkinson's disease (22 assessed in the home environment and 11 in the laboratory) and 31 healthy controls assessed in the laboratory.

In the dopaminergic medication response assessment, 24 people with Parkinson's disease were tested in an 'OFF' state after a minimum 12-hour medication abstinence, and again in an 'ON' state 60 minutes after taking their morning levodopa dose.
Data normality was confirmed using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and Shapiro-Wilk tests, with all Shapiro-Wilk p-values greater than 0.05.
The study did not apply multiple comparison corrections such as the Bonferroni correction, citing the exploratory nature of the investigation.
Analytical validation reliability was assessed using intra-class correlations (ICC2,1), with interpretation thresholds set at poor <0.5, moderate 0.50-0.75, good 0.75-0.90, and excellent >0.90.

Clinical validation known groups validity was examined using an ANOVA with group as a between-subject factor, followed by Tukey post-hoc analysis and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

ROC curve analysis performance was interpreted using Area Under the Curve (AUC) thresholds of outstanding >0.9, excellent 0.8-0.9, good 0.7-0.8, fair 0.6-0.7, and fail <0.5, with optimal cut-off points determined at 100% sensitivity and 0% false positive rate.

Healthy controls (n=31) displayed higher mean OMT frequency than Parkinson's disease patients (n=33) for the right eye (69.65 Hz vs 63.98 Hz), left eye (69.24 Hz vs 63.58 Hz), and both eyes (69.44 Hz vs 63.78 Hz), with p-values <.001 and large effect sizes (Cohen's d=0.88, 1.09, and 0.99 respectively).
Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis for OMT assessment in differentiating Parkinson's disease patients from healthy controls yielded an area under the curve of 0.745-0.773.

In Parkinson's disease patients, lower OMT frequency in the right, left, and both eyes correlated with poorer speech scores on the MDS-UPDRS item 3.1 (r=-.477, p=.005; r=-.367, p=.036; r=-.432, p=.012 respectively).

Test-retest reliability for OMT measures in Parkinson's disease patients showed intraclass correlation coefficients of .94 (95% CI .86-.98) for the right eye, .93 (95% CI .82-.97) for the left eye, and .92 (95% CI .81-.967) for both eyes.

Parkinson's disease patients in the OFF medication state (n=24) and ON medication state (n=24) showed no significant differences in OMT frequency for the right eye (p=.282), left eye (p=.193), or both eyes (p=.158).
The optimal cut-off point for each outcome measure was determined as the point closest to corner (0,1) with a false positive rate of 0% and sensitivity of 100% in the ROC plane.

Convergent validity analysis correlated OMT frequencies with demographic and clinical measures using Pearson's correlation for normally distributed data and Spearman's correlation for non-normally distributed data.
Paired t-tests were performed with medication-state groups ('ON' vs 'OFF' medication) to examine whether OMT reduces when in the 'OFF' medication state in PD.

The analytical validation cohort included 22 participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) who had mild to moderate disease severity and preserved global cognition with a MoCA score of approximately 27.

The clinical validation cohort included 33 participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and 31 healthy controls (HC) who were age-matched, with PwPD having mild to moderate disease severity and a MoCA score of approximately 27.

The response to known intervention cohort included 24 participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) who had mild to moderate disease severity and MoCA scores of approximately 27 when 'OFF' medication and approximately 26 when 'ON' medication.
Test-retest reliability for OMT frequency (Hz) in participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) demonstrated excellent agreement with all intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) greater than 0.90.

The mean difference between first and second visit OMT readings was 1.14 Hz with limits of agreement of 6.6% in the right eye, 1.70 Hz with limits of agreement of 7.4% in the left eye, and 1.73 Hz with limits of agreement of 7.5% in both eyes.

The average OMT frequency for the right eye in healthy controls showed an AUC of 0.745 with a cut-off of 68.58 Hz, sensitivity of 0.818, and 1-specificity of 0.387. The average OMT frequency for the left eye in healthy controls showed an AUC of 0.773 with a cut-off of 65.50 Hz, sensitivity of 0.636, and 1-specificity of 0.258.
The average OMT frequency for both eyes in healthy controls showed an AUC of 0.760 with a cut-off of 65.13 Hz, sensitivity of 0.606, and 1-specificity of 0.226.

In healthy controls, the overall average OMT right eye correlation with age was -0.53 (p=0.002) and with sex was 0.24 (p=0.19). The overall average OMT left eye correlation with age was -0.53 (p=0.002) and with sex was 0.24 (p=0.20).

In people with Parkinson's Disease, the overall average OMT right eye correlation with age was -0.40 (p=0.02) and with sex was 0.27 (p=0.04). The overall average OMT left eye correlation with age was -0.29 (p=0.10) and with sex was 0.38 (p=0.30).
In people with Parkinson's Disease, the overall average OMT both eyes correlation with age was -0.36 (p=0.04) and with sex was 0.39 (p=0.03).

Ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency in the left eye correlated with poorer performance of pronation of the left hand (r = -.380, p = .029) and poorer gait performance (r = -.486, p = .004), while OMT frequency in both eyes correlated with poorer gait performance (r = -.414, p = .017).
No significant differences in OMT readings were observed when participants were 'OFF' and 'ON' anti-Parkinson's medication, a finding consistent across right eye, left eye, and both eye readings.
The OMT measurement using iTremor ONE demonstrated excellent agreement for OMT frequency (Hz) detection with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) greater than 0.9.
The difference in OMT frequency readings between the first and second assessments ranged from 1.13 to 1.72 Hz, representing 1.74% to 2.69% of the average measures.

OMT frequency demonstrated good discriminative ability for differentiating between PwPD and HCs, with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.75 to 0.77 and large effect sizes indicated by Cohen's d values of 0.88 to 1.09.
Across PwPD and HCs, the OMT frequency ranged from approximately 63 to 70 Hz, which is lower than the 68 to 88 Hz range reported in a previous study.

Overall disease severity, measured by UPDRS-III or H&Y stage, did not correlate with OMT frequency, a finding attributed to the limited scoring and subjectivity of these scales compared to the continuous, objective measurement of OMT frequency.

Correlations between OMT frequency and specific UPDRS-III items were observed for speech, facial expression, upper limb movement, and gait, suggesting shared underlying neural processes involving brainstem cholinergic nuclei.
No differences in OMT frequency were detected when participants with Parkinson's disease were tested 'OFF' medication (12-hour washout) compared to 'ON' medication (1 hour after consumption).

In a previous study, one patient with Parkinson's disease showed a reduction in OMT frequency from 78.5 Hz at 24 hours 'ON' medication to 66.5 Hz at 48 hours 'OFF' medication, though these values exceeded the 63-70 Hz range observed in the current study's Parkinson's disease and healthy older adult groups.

The study cohort consisted of a homogeneous mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease group with Hoehn & Yahr stage II-III, lacking stratification by Parkinson's disease phenotype or disease duration. The study was conducted in the North East of England, and unmeasured confounding factors such as caffeine intake, sleep quality, and home environment were not formally recorded.

The statistical analyses were limited to univariate correlational and group comparison approaches, with multivariable modelling recommended for future studies to account for potential confounding variables.

The study included 40 patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease, randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=20) receiving lower-body positive pressure treadmill training or a control group (n=20) receiving conventional physiotherapy, with both groups training twice weekly for 4 months.
Compared to the control group, the experimental group demonstrated significant improvements in gait speed, step length, balance, and postural stability, with all p-values less than 0.01.
The experimental group also showed significant reductions in fear of falling and better quality of life scores compared to the control group, with p-values less than 0.01 for both secondary outcomes.
The prevalence and incidence of Parkinson's disease in Europe are approximately 108-257 per 100,000 and 11-19 per 100,000 persons per year, respectively.
Freezing of gait affects nearly 47% of Parkinson's disease patients.

The study randomized 40 patients in a 1:1 ratio to the experimental group (n=20) or the control group (n=20) after excluding 5 of 45 assessed patients. All 40 participants were included in the final analysis with no losses to follow-up or discontinuations.

The experimental group (n=20) underwent gait training with a 60% body weight reduction applied during each session using the Alter-G system. The control group (n=20) performed a traditional gait training program using a conventional treadmill.

The study enrolled 40 patients with Parkinson's disease (UPDRS score ≤ 81) after excluding 5 of 45 initial candidates (3 for not meeting criteria, 2 for declining participation), with no a priori sample size calculation performed.

Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to an Experimental Group (n=20) or a Control Group (n=20) using a computer-generated simple random sequence without stratification or block randomization.
Blinding of patients and therapists was not feasible due to the intervention nature, but all outcome assessments were performed by evaluators blinded to group allocation to minimize detection bias.
Inclusion criteria required a Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) score ≥ 24 (age- and education-corrected), Hoehn and Yahr stage between II and III, and age between 50 and 85 years.

The Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I) is a 16-item questionnaire with scores ranging from a minimum of 16 to a maximum of 64. The Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39) consists of 39 items grouped into eight domains, with each item scored on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 to 4 and domain scores transformed to a 0-100 scale.

The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) consists of 14 items, each scored on a 5-point scale ranging from 0 to 4, resulting in a total score range of 0 to 56. The stance phase was defined as 60% of the gait cycle and the swing phase as 40% of the gait cycle for stability and efficiency analysis.

The Berg Balance Scale consists of 14 mobility tasks divided into 3 domains, scored on a 5-point Likert scale with a maximum score of 56, where total scores below 45 are associated with a higher risk of falls and scores below 40 are associated with almost a 100% risk of falling.

The Timed Up and Go test assesses the time to rise from a chair, walk 3 meters, turn around, and sit down, with a suggested cut-off point of 13.5 seconds to identify individuals at increased risk of falls.
The 10-Meter Walk Test assesses gait speed in meters per second by recording the total time taken to walk 6 meters.

The Tinetti Gait and Balance Test uses a standardized ordinal scoring system ranging from zero to two, where a score of 18 or lower indicates high risk of falling, scores between 19 and 23 indicate moderate risk, and scores of 24 or higher indicate statistically low risk.

Postural stability was evaluated using the Zebris Medical GmbH platform by recording Center of Pressure length, average velocity, 95% confidence ellipse, and load distribution while patients stood still with eyes open and closed for 10 seconds.
Statistical analysis used a 95% confidence level with a 5% alpha error, setting statistical significance at p<0.05.
The study utilized a small sample size and multiple endpoints, requiring p-values to be interpreted with caution.
Normality of continuous data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test to determine the use of parametric or non-parametric tests.
Inter-group analysis used unpaired Student's t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, while intra-group analysis used paired Student's t-test or Wilcoxon signed rank test.
Spearman's rank correlation was calculated on change scores (Δ = T1 - T0) to explore associations between quality of life, gait analysis scores, and motor scale.
Raw change scores (Δ = T1 - T0) were not analyzed for primary comparisons because they inflate error variance in small samples.

In the experimental group, Mobility showed positive correlations with Gait Profile Score Right (r=0.61, p<0.001) and COP path length (r=0.49, p=0.03), while Emotional Well-Being correlated with step length left (r=0.62, p<0.001) and right (r=0.45, p=0.05).
Swing Phase Left metrics showed correlations with cadence and average gait speed with all r values ≥ 0.53 and p values ≤ 0.02.

Mobility correlated inversely with gait deviation right (r=-0.64, p<0.001), ADL was negatively related to Swing Phase Right (r=-0.59, p=0.01), and cadence was inversely associated with COP path length (r=-0.52, p=0.02).

Figure 2 displays the comparison between baseline (T0) and follow-up (T1) values in the experimental group for gait and balance variables, where asterisks denote statistically significant differences between T0 and T1 (*p<0.05, **p<0.01).
In the intra-group analysis of the experimental group, the EQ5-D score increased significantly from baseline (T0) to post-intervention (T1) with a p-value of 0.03.
The 10-Meters Walk Test (10-MWT) time decreased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1 with a p-value of 0.01.
Timed Up and Go Test (TUG) times for both the right and left sides decreased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1, with p-values of 0.003 for TUG Right and 0.003 for TUG Left.
The Berg Balance Scale (BBS) score increased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1 with a p-value of 0.001.
The 6-Minutes Walk Test (6-MWT) score increased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1 with a p-value of 0.0003.
Tinetti Scale - Balance (TS-B) and Tinetti Scale - Gait (TS-G) scores increased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1, with p-values of 0.03 and 0.02 respectively.
Average Gait speed increased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1 with a p-value of 0.02.
Step Length Right and Step Length Left increased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1, with p-values of 0.001 and 0.004 respectively.
Postural stability metrics Ellipse and Path length CoP decreased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1, both with p-values of 0.04.
The control group did not show any significant improvements between baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1) for the measured outcomes.

Gait parameters including Cadence, Average Gait Speed, Stride width, Gait Deviation Index Right/Left, Gait Profile Score Right/Left, and Step Length Right/Left showed significant improvements in the experimental group compared to controls with p-values less than 0.001.

The study sample comprised 40 subjects, with 20 in the experimental group and 20 in the control group. The global sample included 30 males (75%) and 10 females (25%), with a mean age of 67.18 ± 7.29 years and a mean education level of 2.73 ± 0.99.

Baseline comparisons between the experimental group and control group showed no significant differences in age (p=0.25), sex distribution (p=0.99), or education level (p=0.99). Significant baseline differences were observed in PDQ-39 Mobility (p=0.01), Cognition (p=0.01), Communication (p=0.03), 10-Min Walk Test (p<0.001), and Gait Deviation Index Left (p=0.02).

At T1, the experimental group demonstrated significant improvements over the control group in EQ5-D (p=0.005), Mobility (p=0.007), Communication (p<0.001), FES-I (p<0.001), 10-MWT (p<0.001), TUG Right and Left (p<0.001), BBS (p<0.001), UPDRS-III (p<0.001), HY (p<0.001), and 6-MWT (p<0.001).
Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 with a 5% alpha error, and the authors noted that p-values must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and multiple endpoints.

For the 10MWT, the experimental group had a T0 median of 5.7 (IQR 5.3-7.8) and T1 median of 5.8 (IQR 4.2-6.4), while the control group remained at 5.6 (IQR 5.0-7.4) for both T0 and T1, with a within-group p-value of 0.01 for the experimental group. For TUG-Right, the experimental group improved from a T0 median of 12.3 (IQR 10.1-14.7) to a T1 median of 10.9 (IQR 8.7-14.2), compared to a stable control group median of 11.3 (IQR 8.9-13.4), with a within-group p-value of 0.003 for the experimental group.

For the 6MWT, the experimental group improved from a T0 mean of 300.0 ± 75.6 to a T1 mean of 343.7 ± 87.3, while the control group remained at a median of 280.0 (IQR 217.5-306.7) for both T0 and T1, with a within-group p-value of 0.0003 for the experimental group. For TS-B, the experimental group increased from a T0 median of 14.0 (IQR 12.5-15.0) to a T1 median of 15.0 (IQR 13.7-16.0), compared to a stable control group median of 12.0 (IQR 10.0-14.0), with a within-group p-value of 0.03 for the experimental group.
The study utilized a sample size of n=20 per group, which limits generalizability, and the exploratory nature of the trial increases the risk of Type I error.
Multiple endpoints were assessed in the study, and although appropriate statistical tests were applied, a repeated-measures analysis was not feasible.
The FES-I score at T1 showed a p-value of <0.001 between the experimental and control groups, with a within-group p-value of 0.09 for the experimental group.
The EQ-5D score at T1 showed a p-value of 0.005 between the experimental and control groups, with within-group p-values of 0.03 for the experimental group and 0.12 for the control group.

The PDQ-39 Mobility score at T0 showed a p-value of 0.01 between the experimental and control groups, and the PDQ-39 Cognition score at T0 showed a p-value of 0.01 between the experimental and control groups.
The PDQ-39 Communication score at T1 showed a p-value of 0.0007 between the experimental and control groups.
The statistical analysis employed paired Student's t-tests for parametric data, Wilcoxon signed rank tests for nonparametric data, and Mann-Whitney U tests for nonparametric comparisons.

A single-group study using a paired test with a small sample size (n) produces wide confidence intervals that likely overlap zero, rendering any reported p-value uninterpretable without a control group or correction for multiple comparisons.

The claim that OMT frequency is a distinct biomarker is unsupported because the data only proves measurement consistency under specific conditions using a single device and one operator, failing to establish generalizability or a link to patient outcomes.

The retrospective cohort study utilized a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea, applying propensity score matching to adjust for demographic, clinical, and comorbidity variables.

Competing risk analysis and Cox regression were employed to analyze the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease, accounting for antipsychotic medication exposure and comorbid conditions.

Competing risk analysis and Cox regression were used to analyze the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease, considering antipsychotic medication exposure and comorbid conditions. Individuals with schizophrenia had a significantly higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease than control subjects, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.198.

Among schizophrenia patients, risperidone use was associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease compared with controls, whereas quetiapine use was associated with a reduced risk. Significant comorbidities, including head injury and cerebrovascular disease, also contributed to the increased risk of Parkinson's disease.
A study exploring PD risk factors reported an odds ratio of 4.48 for schizophrenia.

The study used a 1:2 propensity score matching ratio on the Charlson Comorbidity Index score, age, gender, and index year, with a caliper width of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score and a standardized mean difference threshold of 0.1 for imbalance.

Cox regression analysis calculated crude and adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals for Parkinson's disease incidence rates, and survival analysis used the Kaplan-Meier method with significance determined by the log-rank test.

Fine-Gray's competing risk analysis determined the risk of Parkinson's disease considering death as a competing risk factor, and sensitivity analysis was conducted using 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date.

The outcome of incident Parkinson's disease was defined as a new diagnosis using ICD-10 code G20 occurring at least one year after initial schizophrenia diagnosis, requiring at least one inpatient diagnosis or two outpatient diagnoses with the G20 code within a one-year period to minimize diagnostic errors.

Covariates included demographic factors (sex, age, index year), clinical conditions (gastrointestinal diseases, osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis, head injury, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertensive disease, end-stage renal disease, coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease), the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), mental disorders (ICD-10, F00-F69), and related medications (ATC, N05A-N06D) based on records from one year prior to the outcome.

A sensitivity analysis was conducted using time windows of 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date due to limited knowledge about the onset of Parkinson's disease in schizophrenia patients. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide version 9.4 with a two-sided confidence interval of 0.05 considered to indicate statistical significance.

The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Chungbuk National University (CBNU-202204-HR-0068; approval date: 18 April 2022) and utilized de-identified secondary data from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS), for which the requirement for individual informed consent was waived.

A total of 42,522 patients with schizophrenia were matched to 85,041 controls by age, gender, matching-period Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, and index year. The average age of the patients with schizophrenia was 66.26 ± 18.48 years and the average age of the control group was 66.36 ± 18.27 years.

Both the patients with schizophrenia and the control group had a higher proportion of females than males (60.6%), and 53% of patients in each group scored three or more points on the matching-period Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI).

In the univariate analysis, patients with schizophrenia had a significantly higher prevalence of comorbidities, including mental and behavioral disorders, head injuries, COPD, and cerebrovascular disease, compared to control patients. The usage rate of N05A medication was approximately 51% higher among patients with schizophrenia than in the control group.

For the multivariable analysis, variables with a phi coefficient of 0.4 or higher were excluded to ensure reliability, specifically CCI score, medication N05A-N06D, mood (affective) disorders, and hyperlipidemia. In cases of collinearity between a disease and a medication, the medication was excluded.

Competing risk analysis revealed that schizophrenia was associated with a 3.198-fold increased risk of Parkinson's disease (95% CI = 3.126-3.217). The risk of developing Parkinson's disease was higher in males than in females (aHR = 1.103; CI = 1.082-1.126).

In the sensitivity analysis of Parkinson's disease risk by exposure duration, the adjusted hazard ratio for 1 year of exposure was 3.310 (95% CI: 3.238-3.384) in the no competing risk model and 3.198 (95% CI: 3.126-3.217) in the Fine-Gray competing model, with p-values <0.001 for both.

The adjusted hazard ratio for 2 years of exposure was 3.289 (95% CI: 3.217-3.363) in the no competing risk model and 3.147 (95% CI: 3.075-3.221) in the Fine-Gray competing model, with p-values <0.001 for both.

The adjusted hazard ratio for 3 years of exposure was 3.276 (95% CI: 3.204-3.351) in the no competing risk model and 3.118 (95% CI: 3.045-3.193) in the Fine-Gray competing model, with p-values <0.001 for both.

Quetiapine use was associated with a reduced risk of Parkinson's disease (HR: 0.946, 95% CI: 0.899-0.995, p=0.0317), whereas risperidone use was associated with an increased risk (HR: 1.142-1.267, p<0.001).
Aripiprazole use was significantly associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease compared with non-users (HR: 1.160, 95% CI: 1.103-1.221, p<0.001).

Mental and behavioral disorders due to psychoactive substance use (HR: 1.305, 95% CI: 1.218-1.398, p<0.001) and neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders (HR: 1.338, 95% CI: 1.286-1.393, p<0.001) showed the strongest associations with Parkinson's disease risk among comorbidities.
The association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease remained statistically significant after adjusting for relevant covariates, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.198.

Sensitivity analysis including competing risk analysis demonstrated that the adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) for Parkinson's disease remained significant across 1-, 2-, and 3-year periods of comorbidities.

A Kaplan-Meier plot showed a significantly steeper decline in Parkinson's disease-free survival for patients with schizophrenia compared to controls over a 10-year follow-up period, with a log-rank test P-value of <0.0001.
In multivariate analysis, the use of antipsychotic drugs (N05A) was significantly associated with the development of Parkinson's disease with a hazard ratio of 1.076 (95% CI: 1.023-1.132, p=0.0045).

Among comorbidities, neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders showed the highest association with Parkinson's disease development with a hazard ratio of 1.380 (95% CI: 1.333-1.429, p<0.001).
The study cohort consisted of 85,041 control participants and 42,522 patients with schizophrenia, with mean ages of 66.36 ± 18.27 years and 66.26 ± 18.48 years respectively (P=0.40, SMD=0.005).
The mean duration of the index year was 2016.2 ± 3.12 years for the control group and 2016.2 ± 3.11 years for patients with schizophrenia (P=0.07, SMD<0.001).

The Charlson Comorbidity Index score of 0 was observed in 23.56% of the control group and 27.17% of patients with schizophrenia (SMD=0.083), while a score of 3 or higher was observed in 45.16% of the control group and 43.02% of patients with schizophrenia (SMD=0.043).
The prevalence of organic, including symptomatic, mental disorders was 20.43% in the control group and 51.03% in patients with schizophrenia (P<0.001, SMD=0.673).
The prevalence of mood (affective) disorders was 17.98% in the control group and 62.16% in patients with schizophrenia (P<0.001, SMD=1.009).
The prevalence of antipsychotic use (N05A) was 19.56% in the control group and 71.12% in patients with schizophrenia (P<0.001, SMD=1.210).

Patients prescribed antipsychotics had a hazard ratio of 1.258 (95% CI: 1.184-1.337, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease compared to non-users, with Kaplan-Meier plots showing significantly lower PD-free survival rates in the antipsychotic group.
Quetiapine was the most commonly prescribed antipsychotic with 20,485 patients, followed by risperidone with 9,521 patients and aripiprazole with 5,052 patients.
Risperidone use was associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease with a hazard ratio of 1.203 relative to non-users in the subgroup multivariate analysis.

Schizophrenia was associated with a crude hazard ratio of 3.845 (95% CI: 3.772-3.920, p<0.001) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.310 (95% CI: 3.238-3.384, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease in the no competing risk analysis.

Male sex was associated with a crude hazard ratio of 1.201 (95% CI: 1.178-1.224, p<0.001) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.121 (95% CI: 1.099-1.143, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease in the no competing risk analysis.

Neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders were associated with a crude hazard ratio of 1.991 (95% CI: 1.954-2.030, p<0.001) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.508 (95% CI: 1.476-1.541, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease in the no competing risk analysis.

Head injury was associated with a crude hazard ratio of 1.640 (95% CI: 1.561-1.723, p<0.001) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.249 (95% CI: 1.188-1.312, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease in the no competing risk analysis.

Cerebrovascular disease was associated with a crude hazard ratio of 1.307 (95% CI: 1.279-1.336, p<0.001) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.346 (95% CI: 1.314-1.379, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease in the no competing risk analysis.
N05A (Antipsychotics) were associated with a crude hazard ratio of 2.744 (95% CI: 2.692-2.798, p<0.001) for Parkinson's disease in the no competing risk analysis.
Quetiapine was associated with a reduced risk of Parkinson's Disease compared with non-users, whereas risperidone was associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's Disease.

The study found a weak positive association between overall N05A drug exposure and an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (PD). The cohort identified quetiapine, risperidone, and aripiprazole as the three most commonly prescribed N05A drugs, which demonstrated divergent associations with PD risk.

Quetiapine has a higher affinity for serotonin 5-HT2 receptors than for dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, whereas risperidone exhibits a higher dopamine receptor occupancy rate than quetiapine. Aripiprazole is a high-affinity D2 partial agonist with very high D2/3 receptor occupancy at clinically effective doses.

To minimize the misclassification of transient drug-related parkinsonian symptoms as idiopathic PD, the study defined Parkinson's disease as new diagnoses made at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis. This one-year lag period was applied to reduce the possibility that early, reversible medication-induced parkinsonism was misclassified as true degenerative PD.

In the adjusted hazard ratio analysis for Parkinson's Disease among antipsychotic drug prescription patients, antipsychotic drugs were associated with an adjusted HR of 1.076 (95% CI: 1.023-1.132, P = 0.01).
Neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders were associated with an adjusted HR of 1.380 (95% CI: 1.333-1.429, P < 0.001) for Parkinson's Disease in antipsychotic drug prescription patients.

In the adjusted hazard ratio analysis for Parkinson's Disease among quetiapine and risperidone prescription patients, quetiapine exposure was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.946 (95% CI: 0.899-0.995, P = 0.03).

In the adjusted hazard ratio analysis for Parkinson's Disease among quetiapine and risperidone prescription patients, risperidone exposure was associated with a hazard ratio of 1.203 (95% CI: 1.142-1.267, P < 0.001).

A competing risk analysis was conducted to account for the potential impact of premature death before Parkinson's disease onset, and the results of this analysis were consistent with the standard analysis without competing risks.
The study's retrospective observational design limits causal inference, requiring the observed findings to be interpreted as associations rather than definitive evidence of causality.

To improve diagnostic accuracy and address the potential concern of misclassification of diagnoses based on administrative codes, the study defined diseases as requiring at least one inpatient record or two outpatient records within a year.

Multiple comparisons across different antipsychotic agents were not explicitly adjusted, which may increase the risk of Type I error, although potential confounding was addressed by incorporating a wide range of clinical and demographic covariates into the multivariate models.
Medication adherence could not be directly assessed, so an intent-to-treat approach was applied to mitigate this limitation.
The study applied an intent-to-treat approach to mitigate the limitation that medication adherence could not be directly assessed.

Collinearity analysis was conducted to reduce confounding effects by excluding highly correlated variables, though residual bias may persist due to the close association between schizophrenia diagnosis and antipsychotic medication use.

The study could not fully account for time-varying treatment patterns, such as medication switching or the use of anticholinergics, which may lead to misclassifying persistent medication-induced symptoms as incident Parkinson's disease.

A 1-year lag period was used, but the risk of reverse causation remains present given Parkinson's disease's long prodromal phase and the complex temporal relationship between schizophrenia onset, medication exposure, and Parkinson's disease diagnosis.
The study utilized a cohort design with competing risk adjustment and specifically focused on schizophrenia patients while including a wide range of covariates.
The study performed a focused comparison of two antipsychotic medications to explore their differential impacts on Parkinson's disease risk.
The study evaluated the association of schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease using a large claims data including the majority of the Korean population.

The absence of a healthy control group in the study design prevents the isolation of the proposed 'distinct physiological signal' from consistent environmental noise or single-operator protocol artifacts, rendering the biomarker claim invalid regardless of statistical corrections.

Wide confidence intervals render the reported effects uninterpretable, but this statistical limitation is secondary to the design flaw that prevents distinguishing the biological signal from the testing environment baseline.

The lack of provided preprocessing pipeline scripts and parameter settings makes the reported variance impossible to verify, creating a reproducibility black box that undermines the reliability of the measurement tool.

The study demonstrates high measurement reliability but fails to prove clinical utility because the missing control group and unadjusted statistics leave the question of whether the metric predicts patient outcomes completely unresolved.

Even if the Area Under the Curve (AUC) were perfectly corrected for multiple comparisons, the absence of a healthy comparator prevents ruling out that the observed signal is a consistent artifact of the testing environment rather than a biological marker.

The validation study reports an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.77, a metric that is statistically uninterpretable because the confidence interval likely overlaps chance, rendering the reliability metrics untrustworthy due to an unvalidated pipeline.

The rehabilitation trial's efficacy claims are unsupported by definitive numbers due to an exploratory design and small sample size, and independent verification of the force plate readings is blocked by the missing specific code for the anti-gravity treadmill calibration.

The cohort study's risk estimates remain preliminary and impossible to replicate independently because they rely on unadjusted administrative diagnostic codes rather than raw diagnostic metadata, leaving the specific risk estimates uncheckable without access to the raw data.
The uncorrected multiple comparisons in the digital biomarker studies inflate the Type I error rate, and the absence of independent variance estimates renders cross-validation impossible.
Establishing the independent diagnostic value of the digital metrics requires a prospective study with at least n = 100 per group to narrow the 95% confidence interval on the effect size.
