documents: A new handheld device can measure tiny, involuntary eye movements without surgery, and the evidence shows it gives consistent results when used on people with Parkinson's Disease. This means the test is reliable enough to be trusted for checking these specific eye movements.

People with Parkinson's Disease were found to have slower tiny eye movements than healthy people of the same age, but the evidence is not strong enough to say the device can clearly tell the two groups apart on its own. The test does not show that taking Parkinson's medication changes these eye movements.

A new handheld device that uses laser technology to measure tiny eye muscle tremors has been shown to be practical and less invasive than older methods, but it has not yet been proven to be accurate or reliable for people with Parkinson's disease.

This early study aimed to check if the new handheld device can consistently measure eye tremors and if it is practical to use in real-world clinical settings for people living with Parkinson's disease.

A new handheld device can measure a tiny, involuntary eye movement in people with Parkinson's disease quickly and comfortably without any painful procedures. This simple test could help doctors diagnose the condition earlier or monitor how it is progressing.

The eye movement measured by the device is linked to specific symptoms like difficulty with facial expressions and walking, but it does not change when people take standard Parkinson's medications. This suggests the eye movement reflects brain chemistry that is different from the system targeted by current treatments.

Researchers are confident that the new device provides reliable measurements and can accurately distinguish between people with Parkinson's disease and healthy older adults. However, larger studies are still needed to confirm these findings before the test is widely used in clinical practice.

A new quick and comfortable test for measuring tiny, constant eye movements could help doctors diagnose or monitor certain brain and eye conditions earlier. However, larger studies are still needed to confirm that this test works as well as hoped.

Tiny, constant eye movements that happen in everyone at all times may be a sensitive sign of how the brain is functioning, but they cannot be seen without special tools. Current ways to measure these movements are uncomfortable, require numbing the eye, and force patients to keep their eyes open for long periods.

Researchers believe these tiny eye movements are linked to activity in the lower part of the brain, and changes in them have been seen in people with specific neurological diseases. However, the exact parts of the brain responsible for these movements are not yet fully understood.

The study checked if the eye movement test could tell the difference between people with Parkinson's disease and healthy people, but it did not prove the test is accurate enough to use for diagnosing the condition on its own.

Researchers looked at whether the eye movement test changed when people with Parkinson's disease took their morning medication, but the study did not show that the test can reliably measure how well the medication is working.

The study found that the eye movement measurement was highly consistent across repeated tests, meaning the results can be trusted. No participants experienced any negative side effects or problems with the device during the study.

People with Parkinson's disease blink at a noticeably slower rate than healthy people, and this difference is strong enough to be clearly seen. The evidence is very confident that this difference exists, but it does not show that the test can perfectly diagnose the disease in every individual.

In people with Parkinson's disease, those who blink less often tend to have more trouble with their speech and facial movements. This connection suggests that a slower blink rate may reflect worse control of these specific body parts, but it does not prove that the blink rate causes the speech or facial problems.
The new eye measurement tool provides a very reliable and consistent way to track tiny, involuntary eye movements in people with Parkinson's disease.

The study found that taking standard Parkinson's medication did not change the level of these tiny eye movements, meaning the measurement is not affected by whether a person is currently on their medication.
People who had more difficulty with hand movements or walking tended to have lower levels of these tiny eye movements, suggesting the eye measurement reflects overall physical ability.

The eye movement test showed a clear difference between people with Parkinson's disease and healthy people, but the results overlapped enough that the test should be used as a supporting tool for doctors rather than a standalone diagnosis. This finding suggests the test could help in difficult cases where symptoms are unclear, though more research is needed to confirm its role in screening.

Older age is linked to a slower rate of the specific eye movement measured, which is expected as the brain's control systems for eye movement naturally change over time. This means that age affects the results for both people with Parkinson's disease and healthy people, and individual differences can be large.

The study found that a non-invasive eye movement measure was reliable for people with Parkinson's disease and could distinguish them from healthy people, but this measure did not change when people with Parkinson's disease took their medication. The researchers advise caution because the study was small, only included people with mild to moderate disease, and was conducted in one region, so the results may not apply to everyone or other stages of the illness.

The study confirmed that the eye movement measure worked well for people with Parkinson's disease and healthy controls, showing a link between the measure and age and some aspects of disease severity, but it did not show that the measure changed with medication use. The researchers state that more studies are needed to understand the brain mechanisms behind this measure before it can be used in clinical trials or healthcare settings.

The study found that the frequency of a specific eye movement measure did not change when people with Parkinson's disease took their medication compared to when they did not, which suggests that the chemical system usually targeted by Parkinson's drugs is not the main driver of this eye movement. This means the measure might be useful for tracking other aspects of the disease that standard medication does not address, but more research is needed to understand exactly how it works.

Standard clinical scales used to rate the severity of Parkinson's disease did not match the frequency of this eye movement measure, indicating that these common rating tools may miss subtle changes in symptoms that the eye movement test can detect. This suggests that the eye movement test could provide a more sensitive way to monitor specific aspects of the condition that traditional assessments overlook.

The evidence suggests that the eye movement measure is likely linked to the same brain processes that control speech, walking, and facial expressions, which are often early signs of Parkinson's disease. However, the specific brain pathways and chemicals responsible for this connection remain unknown, so the findings are promising but not yet fully understood.

A previous study suggested that Parkinson's medication might affect this eye movement, but the current research found no such effect using a stricter testing method. This discrepancy highlights that earlier findings might have been influenced by how patients were grouped rather than the actual effect of the medication, meaning the true impact of medication on this eye movement is still uncertain.

The study's statistical analysis is too weak to draw firm conclusions because it lacked a comparison group and did not account for the possibility that results could be random chance. Without these safeguards, the reported findings are effectively uninterpretable and cannot be trusted to show a real effect.

A specialized treadmill that reduces body weight helped people with Parkinson's disease walk faster and take longer steps compared to standard physical therapy. This training also improved their balance and stability, making them feel less afraid of falling and improving their overall quality of life.

Nearly half of people with Parkinson's disease experience a condition where their feet seem to stick to the floor, which increases their risk of falling and reduces their independence. Existing medicines and treatments often fail to fully resolve these walking problems, highlighting the need for additional rehabilitation methods.

A pilot study suggests that a specific type of treadmill exercise using air pressure to reduce body weight may help people with Parkinson's disease walk better and feel better about their daily lives, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to confirm this without larger studies.

Freezing of gait, where people with Parkinson's disease suddenly cannot start or continue walking, is a severe problem that significantly increases the risk of falls and reduces independence, and it is often difficult to treat with standard medications.

Using a treadmill that reduces body weight through air pressure allows for safer walking practice with less stress on the joints and a lower risk of falling, which may be especially helpful for people with musculoskeletal pain.

The research was a small, early-stage test meant to gather initial information to guide larger future studies, rather than to provide definitive proof of effectiveness. Because it was a preliminary test, the evidence it provides is not strong enough to make firm conclusions about the treatment.

The study only included people between fifty and eighty-five years old who had a specific diagnosis of Parkinson's disease and experienced difficulty walking. It did not include people with other movement disorders, heart or lung problems, or severe vision or hearing issues, so the results do not apply to those groups.

The people receiving the new treatment and the therapists guiding them knew which group each person was in, which could have influenced the results. However, the people measuring the outcomes did not know which group each person was in, which helps reduce the chance of biased measurements.
The study's findings should be interpreted with caution because the group of people tested was small and many different outcomes were measured.
The study involved a small number of people, so the results should be viewed with caution and are not a definitive proof of the treatment's effect.
People in the experimental group started the study with worse mobility, thinking, and communication skills than those in the control group.
After the treatment, people in the experimental group showed better quality of life, mobility, and balance compared to the control group.
The two groups of people were similar in age, gender, and education level at the start of the study.

The study measured how people with Parkinson's disease felt about the risk of falling during daily activities, with higher scores indicating a stronger fear of falling. This measure is considered a reliable way to assess these specific concerns.

The study evaluated the overall impact of Parkinson's disease on daily living and well-being, where higher scores reflect a greater negative effect on quality of life. This assessment complements other measures by providing a general view of overall health status.

The study assessed the severity of anxiety symptoms in participants, with higher scores indicating more severe anxiety. This tool is widely used by clinicians to measure how strongly anxiety affects a person.

Participants in the treatment group had their walking patterns and muscle activity measured before and after the intervention to track progress. This detailed analysis helps evaluate how well the therapy works and supports monitoring postural stability over time.

The study measured how well people could balance, move, and walk to see if the treatment improved their daily physical abilities. It also checked if the treatment helped people feel less worried about falling and reduced their anxiety.
A specific balance test was used to predict the chance of a person falling, with lower scores indicating a much higher risk of falling.
A walking test was used to measure how far a person could walk in a set time, which gives information about their stamina and heart and lung health.
A test where a person stands up from a chair, walks a short distance, turns around, and sits back down was used to help predict the risk of falling.
The speed at which a person walked a short distance was measured to assess their walking ability.
A standardized test was used to assess balance and walking, where a low score indicates a high risk of falling and a high score indicates a low risk.
A pressure-sensitive platform was used to measure how steady a person stood with their eyes open and closed, providing insights into their balance and how evenly they distributed their weight.

Participants in the experimental group reported feeling healthier and more independent in daily life after the intervention, a change that was not seen in the control group. The evidence strongly supports that the intervention caused these improvements in overall well-being.

People in the experimental group walked faster, moved more easily, and had better balance and endurance compared to their starting point. The evidence is very strong that these physical improvements were caused by the intervention rather than natural changes over time.

The intervention led to better step control, walking efficiency, and reduced body sway for participants in the experimental group. The evidence is strong that these specific improvements in walking and posture were due to the intervention.

The study provides only preliminary evidence that a specific type of treadmill exercise using air pressure may help people with Parkinson's disease walk better, balance more steadily, and feel less afraid of falling. Because the study was small and exploratory, larger studies are needed to confirm these benefits and see if they last over time.

This small pilot study suggests that using a treadmill with body support and air pressure can improve walking speed, step length, balance, and quality of life for people with Parkinson's disease. The findings indicate this method could be a useful addition to standard physical therapy, but more research is required to verify these results in larger groups of patients.

The study found that a specific type of walking therapy helped people with Parkinson's disease balance better and walk with longer steps, which may lower their risk of falling. The evidence is considered preliminary because the study included a small number of people and was designed to explore the treatment rather than prove it works.

People who received the walking therapy reported feeling less afraid of falling and having a better quality of life compared to those who did not. The results suggest that improving physical movement can also help reduce anxiety and improve emotional well-being in people with Parkinson's disease.

The findings do not prove that the therapy works for everyone or that the benefits last long-term, as the study was too small to be certain and did not track participants over an extended period. More large-scale studies are needed to confirm these early results.
Watching actions in a simulated environment helps people practice moving in their minds. The evidence for this benefit is not described in detail here.

Exercises performed in water can help healthy older adults living in the community improve their balance, walking, and quality of life while reducing the risk of falling. The evidence for these benefits is described as a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Walking on a treadmill can help people with Parkinson's disease walk more efficiently on normal ground. This finding comes from a small, controlled pilot study, so the evidence is limited.

Using a special treadmill that moves two belts at different speeds can be used to treat problems with walking. The text does not specify how confident the evidence is or what the treatment does not show.

A specific program of verbal cues can help manage falls in people with Parkinson's disease who experience freezing of gait. This finding is from a feasibility trial, meaning it shows the approach is possible rather than proving it is effective.
A timed test where a person stands up, walks, turns, and sits down provides reliable measurements for people with Parkinson's disease. The text does not explain what this test does not show.
Gait training with body weight support can improve walking and balance for people with incomplete spinal cord injuries. The evidence for this is described as a systematic review with meta-analysis.

Measuring walking patterns with instruments provides information about people with Parkinson's disease that goes beyond standard clinical scales. The text does not explain the confidence in this evidence or what it does not show.

The study's claim that a specific hand tremor rhythm is a unique biological marker is currently unproven because the researchers did not compare the results against a group of healthy people, leaving it unclear if the measurement reflects a real disease signal or just the quirks of the testing equipment.

People living with schizophrenia may face a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, but this link is difficult to confirm because the medications used to treat schizophrenia can also affect the brain in ways that mimic or cause Parkinson's symptoms.
Schizophrenia involves symptoms like seeing or hearing things that are not there and a loss of motivation, which can significantly impact a person's daily life and emotional well-being.

The study looked at whether people with a severe mental health condition were more likely to develop a movement disorder, and whether the medicines used to treat the mental health condition played a role in that development.
The research used health records from a national insurance system in South Korea to track the health of people over a ten-year period.
The study focused on adults who had not been diagnosed with the mental health condition before the start of the tracking period.
Researchers compared people with the mental health condition to people without it, carefully matching the groups by age, gender, and other health factors to make the comparison fair.

The study involved a large group of people with schizophrenia and a separate group of people without the condition who were similar in age, gender, and overall health. Most of the people in both groups were women, and more than half of the people in each group had several other health problems.

People with schizophrenia have a much higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition, and this finding is considered strong. However, this does not show exactly how the mental health condition causes the movement disorder.

Using the medication risperidone is linked to a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, while using quetiapine is linked to a lower chance. This evidence is not strong enough to say for certain that these specific medications cause or prevent the disease.

Doctors should watch closely for signs of Parkinson's disease in people with schizophrenia because of the increased risk. This does not show that the risk will go away if the mental health condition is treated.

Parkinson's disease is a common condition that affects movement and is more common in men than women. The exact cause of the disease is not known, but it is believed to involve a mix of environmental and genetic factors.

People with schizophrenia have a significantly higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition. This link remains strong even after accounting for other health problems and medications.

Men have a slightly higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease than women. Certain other health conditions, such as head injuries and stroke, also increase the risk of developing Parkinson's disease.
People with schizophrenia tend to have more other health problems and take more medications than people without the condition. This includes higher use of specific psychiatric medications.

People living with schizophrenia have a much higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition. This connection remained strong even after accounting for other health factors, suggesting a clear link between the two conditions.

Using the medication quetiapine was linked to a lower chance of developing Parkinson's disease, while using risperidone was linked to a higher chance. The evidence strongly supports that these specific medications have different effects on the risk of developing the disease.

Having mental health conditions related to stress or substance use was associated with a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease. The study found these specific mental health issues were among the strongest factors linked to the development of the disease.

The study found that people with schizophrenia had a significantly shorter time before developing Parkinson's disease compared to those without the condition. This indicates that the onset of Parkinson's disease tends to happen sooner in people who also have schizophrenia.

People taking antipsychotic medications are more likely to develop Parkinson's disease than people who do not take these medications, and the evidence is very strong. This finding does not prove that the medications cause the disease.

People with schizophrenia have a much higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to people without the condition, and the evidence for this link is very strong. This finding does not show that schizophrenia causes Parkinson's disease.
Men are somewhat more likely to develop Parkinson's disease than women, and the evidence for this difference is very strong. This finding does not explain why men are at higher risk.

People with certain stress-related mental health conditions have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, and the evidence for this link is very strong. This finding does not show that these mental health conditions cause Parkinson's disease.

People who have had a head injury are more likely to develop Parkinson's disease, and the evidence for this link is very strong. This finding does not prove that head injuries cause Parkinson's disease.

People with cerebrovascular disease have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, and the evidence for this link is very strong. This finding does not show that cerebrovascular disease causes Parkinson's disease.

People taking the specific antipsychotic medication risperidone have a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease compared to those not taking it, while people taking the antipsychotic medication quetiapine have a slightly lower chance. The evidence for these specific drug effects is considered reliable, but the study does not prove that the medications directly cause the disease.

The study found a link between schizophrenia and a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, but this does not prove that schizophrenia causes Parkinson's disease. The evidence is limited because the study could not track exact medication doses or how long people took the drugs, which makes it hard to fully explain the connection.

The researchers could not determine if patients actually took their medications as prescribed, which limits how certain the findings are about the specific drugs involved. The study also did not look at every single medication separately, only those with enough patient data to analyze.

Researchers caution that the results should be interpreted with care because it is difficult to completely separate the effects of the mental health condition from the effects of the medications used to treat it.

The study is considered valuable because it specifically examined people with schizophrenia in an Asian population and carefully accounted for other health conditions and medications, which previous studies had not done.

The findings suggest that more investigation is needed to understand the connection between the mental health condition and the movement disorder, as well as to determine if higher doses of certain medications increase the risk.

Conditions affecting smell and blood flow in the brain may share underlying causes that increase the risk of developing Parkinson's disease in people with schizophrenia. This evidence suggests that brain inflammation and protein buildup can make the disease more likely, but it does not prove that these conditions directly cause the disease.

Anxiety and stress-related disorders are linked to a higher chance of developing Parkinson's disease, with more severe anxiety correlating to greater risk. These mental health issues may act as early warning signs or amplify the damage to the brain, though the exact connection remains uncertain.

Antipsychotic medications used to treat schizophrenia show a weak overall link to Parkinson's disease, but specific drugs like quetiapine and risperidone affect the brain differently. While some symptoms may reverse if the medication is stopped, long-term use might still lead to permanent brain damage, though the evidence for this specific outcome is not definitive.

The reported accuracy of the digital tool is statistically uninterpretable because the range of possible true values likely includes no benefit, suggesting the signal might just be the software fitting to its own errors instead of detecting a real health condition.

The central claims of the research cannot be verified because the missing details on how the data was processed and the medical codes used create a fragmented picture where only the broadest trends are reliable.

For people living with this condition, the new diagnostic tools are not yet ready to replace current medical advice because the science has not proven these methods work reliably for real people. Patients should not stop or change their existing treatment based on these preliminary findings.

The new digital tools for tracking movement are not ready to replace your current doctor's advice because the evidence is too weak to be trusted. This means the science needs more time to prove these methods work for real people before they can guide your care.

The current evidence leaves open the fundamental issue of whether the movement frequency metric reflects a true physiological marker or just experimental noise. We need to see this integrated with established clinical measures in larger trials before it can move from an interesting research trend to a validated diagnostic tool.

The current digital health tools cannot reliably tell a patient if their condition is improving or worsening because they lack a comparison group of healthy people to establish what is normal. Until a new study properly compares these tools against healthy baselines, they offer no trustworthy information about a patient's actual health status.

documents: The study dataset is pseudo-anonymized and cannot be publicly deposited because it was collected from NHS patients under ethics approval REF: 23/WM/0004 and Northumbria University ethics Project No. 0034.
The study used the hand-held device iTremor ONE to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) in 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease and 31 age-matched healthy controls.

Analytical validation involved a test-retest reliability assessment on 22 participants with Parkinson's Disease, and clinical validation compared OMT frequency in 33 participants with Parkinson's Disease to controls.
A medication comparison subgroup consisted of 24 participants with Parkinson's Disease who were tested in 'OFF' (12-hour withdrawal) and 'ON' anti-Parkinson's (dopaminergic) medication states.

Data for the study are available from Northumbria University's Data Protection Officer upon reasonable request via email dp.officer@northumbria.ac.uk, telephone 0191243 7357, or mail to the Data Protection Officer at Pandon Building, Northumbria University, Newcastle Upon Tyne, NE1 8ST. The study utilized the iTremor ONE device provided by Head Diagnostics, which measures ocular microtremor non-invasively in three seconds using laser technology.

The research was supported by a collaborative PhD studentship between Northumbria University and Head Diagnostics awarded to Lisa Graham, as well as grants from the Parkinson's Foundation with identifiers PF-FBS-1898 and PF-CRA-2073.
The study utilizes the iTremor ONE device (Head Diagnostics Ltd., Dublin, Ireland), which employs laser technology to measure Ocular Motor Tremor (OMT) frequency in Hertz.

A critical gap for replication is that the iTremor ONE device has not yet undergone analytical and clinical validation to determine its accuracy, reliability, and sensitivity for Parkinson's Disease populations.

The analytical validation objectives are to investigate the test-retest reliability of the iTremor ONE for measuring OMT frequency in people with Parkinson's Disease and to assess the feasibility of using this hand-held technology in a real-world clinical setting.
The full protocol for the OMT measurement study is available at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0313452.
The study was registered with Clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06051877 and received NHS Research Ethics Committee approval REF: 23/WM/0004.
PwPD participants were included if they met UK brain bank criteria for a PD diagnosis, and healthy controls were required to be aged 50 years old or above.
Participants were excluded from the study if they had a MoCA score of less than 21, indicating severe cognitive impairment.
Ocular microtremor (OMT) oscillates at 70-150 Hz in healthy subjects and cannot be detected by naked eye or standard video-based eye-tracking systems due to insufficient sensitivity.
There is no gold standard technique for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT), which limits the generalisability and interpretation of underlying deficits across different measurement protocols.

Existing invasive methods for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT), such as piezoelectric strain gauges, accelerometer fixed contact lenses, or eyelid fixed accelerometers, require eye anaesthetisation, specialist laboratory space, highly trained operators, and constant uninterrupted contact with the sclera for up to 60 minutes.

The piezoelectric strain gauge technique for measuring ocular microtremor (OMT) possesses high interobserver variability, causes discomfort and eye dryness, and has an unknown loading effect of the probe that makes validation of new techniques against it undesirable.
Ocular motor tremor was measured using the iTremor ONE device from Head Diagnostics Ltd. with software version 0.19, which records data over three seconds per eye after alignment.

The iTremor ONE device measures angular displacement via laser speckle correlation in the Fourier plane of a lens and applies band-pass filtering to segregate ocular motor tremor from other eye movements, hand movements, and head movements.
Twenty-two participants with Parkinson's disease underwent two home-based assessments exactly one week apart at the same time of day within a 30-minute window and in the same home location.
Disease severity was assessed in the "ON" state one hour after Levodopa medication intake using the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's disease Rating scale part III (UPDRS-III).
Participants sat in a high-backed chair with curtains closed to dim light and removed glasses or contact lenses before recording.

The recording involved a low-level laser directed at the sclera for approximately three seconds while participants maintained a relaxed gaze at a wall target at eye level, with readings repeated if the participant blinked.
Three readings were taken for each eye and averaged, using a single iTremor ONE device operated by the same individual for every measurement.

The analytical validation cohort consisted of 22 participants with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) with mild to moderate disease severity and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of approximately 27. The clinical validation cohort included 33 PwPD participants and 31 healthy controls (HC), with the PwPD group age-matched to the control group and exhibiting mild to moderate disease severity and a MoCA score of approximately 27.

The response to known intervention cohort comprised 24 PwPD participants with mild to moderate disease severity and preserved global cognition, with MoCA scores of approximately 27 when 'OFF' medication and approximately 26 when 'ON' medication.

Test-retest reliability for OMT frequency (Hz) at home visits demonstrated excellent agreement with all Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) greater than 0.90. The mean difference between first and second visit readings was 1.14 Hz for the right eye (Limits of Agreement 6.6%), 1.70 Hz for the left eye (Limits of Agreement 7.4%), and 1.73 Hz for both eyes (Limits of Agreement 7.5%).

No adverse events or device issues were recorded during the study, though OMT measurements were occasionally repeated by the examiner if the iTremor ONE device reported an inability to take a reading due to eye blinks, obstruction from eyelashes or eyelids, or changes in gaze direction.
The study used a single iTremor ONE device operated by the same trained operator for all measurements, with readings taken for each eye and averaged.
Clinical validation involved 33 people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) (22 assessed at home, 11 in the laboratory) and 31 healthy controls (HCs) assessed in the laboratory.
Participants were seated in a high-backed chair looking at a target at eye level in a quiet environment with controlled room lighting, and three measures per eye were averaged for all OMT readings.

For medication response testing, 24 PwPD participants abstained from dopaminergic medication for a minimum of 12 hours prior to the 'OFF' state assessment, then took their morning dose and waited 60 minutes before the 'ON' state assessment.
Data were analyzed using SPSS version 28 (IBM Inc, IL, USA), with normal distribution confirmed via Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests (all Shapiro-Wilk p>.05).

OMT frequency outcomes were assessed as an average overall and separately for left and right eyes, with invalid readings treated as missing data and excluded from analysis using available case analysis.

Reliability between visit 1 and visit 2 was assessed using intra-class correlations (ICC2,1), interpreted as poor <0.5, moderate 0.50-0.75, good 0.75-0.90, and excellent >0.90, alongside Pearson's correlations and Bland-Altman graphs.

Known groups validity was examined using ANOVA with group (PwPD vs. HCs) as a between-subject factor, followed by Tukey post-hoc analysis and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis to calculate area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity.
The optimal cut-off point for each outcome measure was determined as the point closest to the (0,1) corner in the ROC plane with a false positive rate of 0% and sensitivity of 100%.

Table 2 reports the Area Under the Curve (AUC), cut-off frequency in Hz, sensitivity, and 1-specificity for Average Ocular Microtremor (OMT) Frequency in the right eye, left eye, and both eyes for differentiating People with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD) from Healthy Controls (HCs).

Table 3 presents Pearson correlation coefficients (r) and p-values for the relationship between Overall Average OMT frequency (right eye, left eye, and both eyes) and clinical measures including Age, Sex, Disease Duration, UPDRS, H&Y, FES-I, nFOGQ, and LEDD for both Healthy Controls (HCs) and People with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD).
The study used the iTremor ONE technology to measure ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency in Hz, demonstrating excellent agreement (ICC > 0.9) for OMT frequency detection.

The study found no significant differences in ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency readings when participants with Parkinson's Disease were 'OFF' versus 'ON' anti-Parkinson's medication, a result consistent across right eye, left eye, and both eye readings.

The study reported correlations between specific motor features and ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency, including a correlation between poorer left hand pronation performance (Item 3.6) and lower OMT frequency in the left eye (r = -.380, p = .029).
The study reported a correlation between poorer gait performance (Item 3.10) and lower ocular microtremor (OMT) frequency in the left eye (r = -.486, p = .004) and in both eyes (r = -.414, p = .017).

Healthy controls (n=31) had a mean OMT frequency of 69.65 Hz (SD=7.33) in the right eye, 69.24 Hz (SD=5.75) in the left eye, and 69.44 Hz (SD=6.47) in both eyes, while participants with Parkinson's disease (n=33) had a mean OMT frequency of 63.98 Hz (SD=5.38) in the right eye, 63.58 Hz (SD=4.58) in the left eye, and 63.78 Hz (SD=4.82) in both eyes.
The OMT assessment achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.745-0.773 in ROC curve analysis for differentiating participants with Parkinson's disease from healthy controls.

In the Parkinson's disease group, OMT frequency in the right, left, and both eyes correlated with MDS-UPDRS item 3.1 (speech) with correlation coefficients of r=-.477 (p=.005), r=-.367 (p=.036), and r=-.432 (p=.012) respectively.

The study participants had a mean age of 69.06 years (SD=7.56) for the Parkinson's disease group and 67.32 years (SD=9.92) for the healthy control group, with a mean UPDRS III score of 35.94 (SD=17.71) for the Parkinson's disease group.

The iTremor ONE device measured OMT frequency with a range of approximately 63-70Hz in PwPD and HCs, which is lower than the 68-88Hz range reported in previous studies using piezoelectric methods, potentially due to technical differences in accuracy.
The study did not control for day-to-day fluctuations in hours of sleep, stress, or caffeine intake, which are identified as sources of variance in OMT frequency measurements.
A previous study using the Piezoelectric method found that caffeine intake caused a small but significant increase in OMT frequency that persisted up to 90 minutes after consumption.

The study reported no adverse events and no participant withdrawals, with minor factors such as blinking or eye movement impacting data collection but resulting in no data loss due to repeated measurements within the session.

The OMT frequency difference between the first and second assessment was between 1.13-1.72Hz, representing 1.74-2.69% of the average measures, which the authors consider normal variation but note requires investigation in a larger population to establish expected day-to-day variation.
The study used a standard 12-hour washout period to test OMT frequency 'OFF' medication and 1 hour after consumption to test 'ON' medication.
A previous study categorized patients into 'ON' or 'OFF' groups based on the bradykinesia section of the Webster Scale rather than a medication washout period.
A single patient in a previous study had OMT frequency recordings of 78.5 Hz 24 hours after medication and 66.5 Hz 48 hours after medication withdrawal due to hypertension.
The current study reported OMT frequency readings in the range of approximately 63-70 Hz for people with Parkinson's disease and healthy older adults.

The study cohort consisted of a homogeneous mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease group (Hoehn & Yahr stage II-III) with no stratification by PD phenotype (e.g., tremor-dominant vs. akinetic-rigid subtypes) or disease duration, and was conducted in the North East of England, limiting generalisability.
Key confounding factors such as caffeine intake, sleep quality, and home environment were not formally recorded in the study.
Statistical analyses were limited to univariate correlational and group comparison approaches, with no multivariable modelling employed to account for potential confounding variables.

The study provides analytical and clinical validation evidence for the iTremor ONE device, specifically noting that OMT frequency was reliably measured and differentiated between Parkinson's disease patients and healthy controls.
Supporting information for the study includes S1 Table (Missing Cases) and S1 Fig (Bland Altman Plots), both provided as DOCX files.

The study reports an intraclass correlation coefficient greater than 0.9 for OMT frequency under the single-operator protocol, providing the specific reliability metric necessary to validate the test-retest consistency of the acquisition pipeline.

Replication is currently blocked by the absence of raw data, analysis scripts, and specific software versions, as well as the lack of disclosed preprocessing parameters and sequence timing details required to reconstruct the analysis pipeline.

The statistical validity of the results is compromised by the use of a single timepoint baseline without a control group or correction for multiple comparisons, rendering any reported p-values uninterpretable due to likely wide confidence intervals overlapping zero.
The study utilized the Alter-G Anti-Gravity Treadmill, which uses differential air pressure technology to reduce body weight during ambulation.
The primary outcome of the randomized controlled trial was the number of freezing of gait (FoG) episodes and gait cycle quality in individuals with Parkinson's disease.
Secondary outcomes measured in the trial included cadence, step length, walking speed, pain, mood, and overall quality of life.
The study data are available from the Ethics Committee (contact via 09060128109) for researchers who meet the criteria for access to confidential data.
The study was supported by Current Research Funds 2025, RRC-2025-23686388.

Forty patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=20) receiving gait training with a lower-body positive pressure treadmill, or to a control group (n=20) undergoing conventional physiotherapy.
Both the experimental group and the control group trained twice weekly for 4 months.
Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1).

The experimental group (n=20) used the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA) with a 60% body weight reduction applied during each session, while the control group (n=20) used a conventional treadmill.

The intervention consisted of 20 sessions (2 times a week for 4 months), each lasting approximately 60 minutes and comprising a 15-minute warm-up, treadmill training on a zero-degree incline, and a 15-minute cooldown.

Initial treadmill speeds were based on baseline gait analysis and were gradually increased over the 20 sessions to reach each participant's maximum walking capacity while ensuring proper gait performance.
The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino Pulejo" (approval number U224/22), and all participants provided signed informed consent.
The study enrolled 40 patients with Parkinson's Disease from IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino-Pulejo" in Messina, Italy, between May 2021 and March 2023, registered as Clinical Trial NCT0574025.

Inclusion criteria required a diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease per Movement Disorder Society Clinical Diagnostic Criteria, evidence of Freezing of Gait, age 50-85 years, Hoehn and Yahr stage II-III, Mini Mental State Examination score of 24 or higher, and absence of musculoskeletal disorders, visual/auditory impairments, or cardiovascular/pulmonary diseases.

Exclusion criteria included the presence of a pacemaker or infusion systems such as Duodopa gel via J-Peg system, comorbidities contraindicating physical exercise, and severe visual or auditory impairment.

Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio using a computer-generated simple random sequence from random.org without stratification or block randomization, assigning 20 patients to the Experimental Group and 20 to the Control Group.

The Experimental Group received body weight-supported treadmill training using differential air pressure combined with conventional therapy, while the Control Group underwent only traditional physical exercise.

The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of IRCCS Centro Neurolesi "Bonino Pulejo" under protocol U224/22, and all outcome assessments were performed by evaluators blinded to group allocation.

The experimental group used the AlterG anti-gravity treadmill model M320 (AlterG, Inc., Fremont, CA, USA), which applies lower-body positive pressure to support 20% to 100% of body weight in 1% increments.

Postural stability was evaluated using the Zebris Medical GmbH platform by recording Center of Pressure (CoP) length, average velocity, 95% confidence ellipse, and load distribution while patients stood still with eyes open and closed for 10 seconds.

Gait parameters were analyzed at T0 and T1 using the BTS Gaitlab, which includes motion capture systems, force platforms, and electromyographic sensors, following the DAVIS protocol with reflective markers and EMG sensors.
The 10-Meter Walk Test recorded the total time taken to walk 6 meters to assess gait speed in meters per second.
The Timed Up and Go test assessed the time to rise from a chair, walk 3 meters, turn around, and sit down, with a cut-off point of 13.5 seconds used to identify increased fall risk.
The study used R version 4.2.2 for statistical analysis, setting a 95% confidence level, a 5% alpha error, and statistical significance at p<0.05.

The protocol extracted specific outcomes including kinematics (hip, knee, ankle, and pelvic joint angles), kinetics (joint moments and powers), electromyography timing for tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, quadriceps, and hamstrings, spatiotemporal parameters (cadence, step width, step length, stance and swing phases, gait speed), and Gait Deviation Index (GDI) and Gait Profile Score (GPS).
Participants performed standing and walking trials at a self-selected comfortable speed with surface EMG electrodes applied to major lower-limb muscles based on standard anatomical landmarks.

The study did not analyze raw change scores (Δ=T1-T0) due to known inflation of error variance in small samples, but used Δ to calculate Spearman's rank correlation for associations between quality of life, gait analysis scores, and motor scale.

Normality of continuous data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, with normally distributed data analyzed via parametric tests (unpaired or paired Student's t-test) and non-normally distributed data analyzed via non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon signed rank test).

Quantitative gait analysis was conducted at baseline (T0) and after treatment (T1) using the BTS Gait Lab (BTS Bioengineering, Milan, Italy), which includes infrared cameras, force plates, and wireless electromyographic sensors.

Data acquisition followed the DAVIS multifactorial protocol, which combines kinematic, kinetic, and electromyographic assessments using reflective markers on standard anatomical landmarks and surface EMG electrodes on major lower-limb muscles.

Participants performed standing and walking trials at a self-selected comfortable speed, with specific parameters recorded including cadence, step width, step length, stance and swing phases, average speed, Gait Deviation Index (GDI), and Gait Profile Score (GPS).
The Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I) is a 16-item questionnaire measuring fear of falling, with scores ranging from a minimum of 16 (no concern) to a maximum of 64 (strong concern).

The Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39) consists of 39 items grouped into eight domains, where each item is scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 0 (never) to 4 (always) and domain scores are transformed to a 0-100 scale.

The Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) is a clinician-administered tool consisting of 14 items, each scored on a 5-point scale from 0 (not present) to 4 (very severe), with a total score range of 0 to 56.
The study utilized a sample size of n=20 per group, which limits generalizability, and a repeated-measures analysis was not feasible due to the assessment of multiple endpoints.
The LLBP therapy treadmill allows precise, incremental unloading of body weight while preserving natural gait kinematics to facilitate gait training.
Secondary outcomes were measured at T0 (baseline) and T1 (post-treatment) using the FES-I, EQ-5D, PDQ-39 subscales, and HAM-A scales.
Data for normally distributed variables were presented as means ± standard deviations, while non-normally distributed variables were presented as medians with first and third quartiles.
Statistical analysis employed the paired Student's t-test for parametric data, the Wilcoxon signed rank test for nonparametric data, and the Mann-Whitney U test for nonparametric comparisons.

The study sample comprised 40 subjects (20 in the Experimental Group and 20 in the Control Group) with a mean age of 67.18 ± 7.29 years, 75% male, and a mean disease duration of 12 ± 8 years. Baseline demographic homogeneity was confirmed for age, sex, and education level, while significant baseline differences existed in PDQ-39 Mobility, Cognition, and Communication scores.

Primary motor outcomes were measured at T0 (baseline) and T1 (post-treatment), with data presented as means ± standard deviations for normally distributed variables and medians (first and third quartiles) for non-normally distributed variables. Specific baseline and post-treatment values for the 10MWT, TUG-Right, TUG-Left, BBS, 6MWT, TS-B, and TS-G are provided in Table 2 with associated p-values for group and time effects.

Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 with a 5% alpha error, and the authors note that p-values must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and multiple endpoints. The DOI for the demographic data table is https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0341021.t001.
The full correlation results are provided in Supplementary S1 Fig and Table 3.
Figure 2 displays baseline (T0) and follow-up (T1) values for gait and balance variables, where bars represent the median and error bars indicate the interquartile range (IQR).
Figure 2 uses asterisks to denote statistically significant differences between T0 and T1, with *p<0.05 and **p<0.01.

The legend for Figure 2 defines the following abbreviations: SP/R=Stance Phase Right, SP/L=Stance Phase Left, SwP/R=Swing Phase Right, SwP/L=Swing Phase Left, CT=Cadence, AGS=Average Gait Speed, SW=Step Width, GDI/R=Gait Deviation Index Right, GDI/L=Gait Deviation Index Left, GPS/R=Gait Profile Score Right, GPS/L=Gait Profile Score Left, SL/R=Step Length Right, SL/L=Step Length Left, CoPL=Center of pressure-Path length, CoPV=Center of pressure-Average velocity, EA=Ellipse, FFR=Foot Force Right, FFL=Foot Force Left, CoPL-CE=Center of pressure-Path Length-closed eyes, CoPV-CE=Center of pressure-average velocity-closed eyes, EA-CE=Ellipse-closed eyes, FFR-CE=Foot Force Right-closed eyes, FFL-CE=Foot Force Left-closed eyes.

The study's supporting information includes S1 Fig (a Spearman's rank correlation matrix between clinical outcomes and gait/balance parameters in the experimental group), S1 File (SPIRIT checklist), and S2 File (Protocol).

The study's supporting information defines specific abbreviations for gait and balance parameters, including CT (Cadence), AGS (Average Gait Speed), GDI/R and GDI/L (Gait Deviation Index Right/Left), GPS/R and GPS/L (Gait Profile Score Right/Left), SL/R and SL/L (Step Length Right/Left), COPL (Center of pressure- Path length), COPV (Center of pressure- Average velocity), and AF/R and AF/L (Average forces right/left).

The study's supporting information defines specific abbreviations for closed-eyes balance parameters, including COPL-CE (Center of pressure- Path Length- closed eyes), COPV-CE (Center of pressure- average velocity- closed eyes), Accuracy-CE (accuracy - closed eyes), AFR-CE (Average_forces_dx_eyes_closed), and AFL-CE (Average_forces_sx_eyes_closed).

The study's acquisition protocol specified three averaged readings per eye to stabilize the signal, but the preprocessing pipeline details are missing, specifically whether bandpass filtering or motion correction was applied before calculating the 1.13 to 1.72 Hz variance.

The methods section omits the specific bandpass filter bands and the exact motion correction algorithm used prior to extracting the 1.13 to 1.72 Hz variance, creating a critical gap that prevents verification of whether the OMT frequency reflects sensor jitter or subtle drift in the iTremor ONE unit.

Replicating the reported variance requires the exact code and parameter settings for the data cleaning step, which are currently absent, rendering the numerical results unverifiable until these scripts are made public.

The study design lacks a control group, which is a fundamental gap that prevents the isolation of the physiological signal from baseline noise and blocks the empirical demonstration that the metric is distinct.

Researchers who meet the criteria for accessing confidential NHIS data may apply for access through the NHIS Data Sharing Service website (https://nhiss.nhis.or.kr). Access to the NHIS dataset is granted only for a predefined period approved for each research project, and once this period has expired, re-access to the same dataset may not be available.

The study is a retrospective cohort study designed to evaluate the risk of Parkinson's disease associated with schizophrenia and the influence of antipsychotic medications prescribed at the time of schizophrenia diagnosis on Parkinson's disease development.

The study design requires careful analysis to exclude confounding drug effects, as Parkinson's disease treatment involves medications such as levodopa that increase dopamine levels, whereas schizophrenia treatment uses dopamine antagonists to reduce dopamine activity.

The de-identified claims data used in the study were obtained from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of Korea and are not publicly available due to NHIS data protection regulations and internal data-use policies.
The retrospective cohort study utilized a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea containing patients diagnosed with schizophrenia and matched controls.

The study employed propensity score matching and adjusted for demographic, clinical, and comorbidity variables using competing risk analysis and Cox regression to analyze the relationship between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.

All statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA), with a two-sided confidence interval of 0.05 considered to indicate statistical significance.

The study utilized de-identified secondary data provided by the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) and was conducted within the NHIS-controlled secure research environment with restricted access, where remote access from personal computers or external networks was not permitted.
A total of 42,522 patients with schizophrenia were matched to 85,041 controls by age, gender, matching-period CCI score, and index year.

The study data were accessed on July 11, 2022, and are available from the National Health Insurance Sharing Service of South Korea, but individual-level data cannot be publicly released due to regulatory restrictions.

The study utilized a customized database from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of South Korea covering 2010 to 2021, which includes demographic characteristics, health insurance claim codes, ICD-10 data, health examination data, and socioeconomic data.

Schizophrenia was defined using ICD-10 code F2* with a requirement of one inpatient record or two outpatient records within one year, while patients diagnosed in 2010 and those under 18 years of age were excluded.

Patients with schizophrenia were matched with controls in a 1:2 ratio using propensity score matching based on the Charlson Comorbidity Index score, age, gender, and index year, with a caliper width of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score.
The end date for the study period was defined as the date of Parkinson's disease diagnosis, death, or the last day of data collection, which was December 31, 2021.

The outcome of incident Parkinson's disease was defined as a new diagnosis using ICD-10 code G20 occurring at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis, requiring at least one inpatient diagnosis or two outpatient diagnoses with the G20 code within a one-year period to minimize diagnostic errors.

Covariates included demographic factors (sex, age, index year), specific clinical conditions (gastrointestinal diseases, osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis, head injury, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertensive disease, end-stage renal disease, coronary heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease), the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), mental disorders (ICD-10, F00-F69), and related medications (ATC, N05A-N06D).

Covariates were derived from records from one year prior to the outcome, and the study end date was defined as the date of Parkinson's disease diagnosis, death, or the last day of data collection (December 31, 2021).

Statistical methods included t-tests for continuous variables, chi-squared tests for binary variables, the phi correlation coefficient for binary associations, Cox regression analysis for crude and adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank tests, and Fine-Gray's competing risk analysis treating death as a competing risk factor.

Sensitivity analysis was conducted using time windows of 1, 2, or 3 years before the end date, and the relationship between antipsychotic medications and Parkinson's disease development was investigated using the intent-to-treat method with Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and log-rank tests based on medications prescribed at the time of the initial diagnosis.

Variables with a phi coefficient of 0.4 or higher were excluded from the multivariable analysis, specifically CCI score, medication N05A-N06D, mood (affective) disorders, and hyperlipidemia. In cases of collinearity between a disease and a medication, the medication was excluded, and in cases of collinearity between two diseases, the disease with more associations with other variables was excluded.

The study reported a 3.198-fold increased risk of Parkinson's disease for schizophrenia (95% CI = 3.126-3.217) and a higher risk for males compared to females (aHR = 1.103; CI = 1.082-1.126). The study flow chart is provided at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0346233.g001.

The study cohort included 85,041 control participants and 42,522 patients with schizophrenia, with baseline characteristics detailed in Table 1 including mean age (66.36 ± 18.27 for controls, 66.26 ± 18.48 for schizophrenia patients) and index year (2016.2 ± 3.12 for controls, 2016.2 ± 3.11 for schizophrenia patients).

Multivariate analysis reported a hazard ratio of 1.076 (95% CI: 1.023-1.132, p=0.0045) for the association between the use of antipsychotic drugs (ATC code N05A) and the development of Parkinson's disease.

Among comorbidities, neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders showed the highest association with Parkinson's disease development, with a hazard ratio of 1.380 (95% CI: 1.333-1.429, p<0.001).

Sensitivity analysis including competing risk analysis confirmed that the adjusted hazard ratio for Parkinson's disease remained significant across 1-, 2-, and 3-year periods of comorbidities, as presented in Table 3.

The Kaplan-Meier plot of Parkinson's disease-free survival rates indicated a significantly steeper decline for patients with schizophrenia compared to controls over the 10-year follow-up period, with a log-rank test p-value of <0.0001.

The study used Cox proportional regression and Fine-Gray competing risk analysis to calculate crude and adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for Parkinson's disease, with specific adjusted HRs reported for schizophrenia (3.310, 95% CI: 3.238-3.384) and male sex (1.121, 95% CI: 1.099-1.143). The analysis adjusted for variables including age (adjusted HR 0.990, 95% CI: 0.989-0.990) and the Charlson Comorbidity Index.

Quetiapine was the most commonly prescribed antipsychotic with 20,485 patients, followed by risperidone with 9,521 patients and aripiprazole with 5,052 patients. Risperidone use was significantly associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease with a hazard ratio of 1.203 in the subgroup multivariate analysis.

The adjusted hazard ratio for Parkinson's disease associated with the use of N05A (Antipsychotics) was 2.744 (95% CI: 2.692-2.798) in the no competing risk analysis, while the adjusted HR for N06B (Psychostimulants for ADHD) was 1.958 (95% CI: 1.895-2.023). The study also reported adjusted HRs for comorbidities such as neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders (1.508, 95% CI: 1.476-1.541) and head injury (1.249, 95% CI: 1.188-1.312).

Table 4 reports adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's Disease in antipsychotic drug prescription patients, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.076 (95% CI 1.023-1.132, P=0.01) for antipsychotic drugs and 0.983 (95% CI 0.982-0.984, P<0.001) for age.

Table 5 reports adjusted hazard ratios for Parkinson's Disease in quetiapine and risperidone prescription patients, with a hazard ratio of 0.946 (95% CI 0.899-0.995, P=0.03) for quetiapine and 1.203 (95% CI 1.142-1.267, P<0.001) for risperidone.
The study utilized a retrospective cohort from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database in South Korea to investigate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease (PD).

Table 3 presents sensitivity analysis results for PD risk by exposure duration using both a no competing risk model and a Fine-Gray competing model, with adjusted hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) provided for 1, 2, and 3-year durations.
Variables with a Phi correlation coefficient greater than 0.4 were excluded from the adjusted hazard ratio analysis, and comorbidities were matched in the same period as the exposure.

The analysis reported specific hazard ratios for antipsychotic use, where quetiapine use was associated with a reduced risk of PD (HR: 0.946, 95% CI: 0.899-0.995) and aripiprazole use was associated with an increased risk of PD (HR: 1.160, 95% CI: 1.103-1.221).

Comorbidities identified with the strongest associations with PD included mental and behavioral disorders due to psychoactive substance use (HR: 1.305, 95% CI: 1.218-1.398) and neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders (HR: 1.338, 95% CI: 1.286-1.393).

The primary finding indicated that individuals with schizophrenia had a higher risk of developing PD than those without, with an adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 3.198 after adjusting for relevant covariates.

The study reports specific hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals and p-values for end-stage renal disease (0.802, 0.732-0.878, p<0.001), coronary heart disease (0.927, 0.879-0.979, p=0.01), and cerebrovascular disease (1.130, 1.080-1.182, p<0.001) in relation to Parkinson's disease risk.

The analysis compares event-free survival for Parkinson's disease among patients using quetiapine, risperidone, and non-users, with quetiapine associated with reduced risk and risperidone with increased risk compared to non-users.

The study defined Parkinson's disease as new diagnoses made at least one year after the initial schizophrenia diagnosis to minimize the misclassification of transient, drug-related parkinsonian symptoms as idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
Quetiapine has a higher affinity for serotonin 5-HT2 receptors than for dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, while risperidone exhibits a higher dopamine receptor occupancy rate than quetiapine.
Aripiprazole is a high-affinity D2 partial agonist where molecular imaging studies indicate that D2/3 receptor occupancy can be very high at clinically effective doses.
The study utilized a large claims database containing data for the majority of the Korean population to evaluate the association between schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.
The study applied a 1-year lag period between exposure and outcome to mitigate the risk of reverse causation.
The study employed a cohort design with competing risk adjustment and included a wide range of clinical and demographic covariates in multivariate models.
The study performed a focused comparison of two specific antipsychotic medications to explore their differential impacts on Parkinson's disease risk.
The study utilized an intent-to-treat approach to mitigate limitations regarding the inability to directly assess medication adherence.
Collinearity analysis was conducted to reduce confounding effects by excluding highly correlated variables from the models.
The study relied on administrative claims data which lacked granular clinical information such as disease severity, symptom onset timing, and neuroimaging results (e.g., DaTscan).
The analytical framework of the large-scale administrative database prevented the reflection of individual daily dosing ranges or the exact cumulative duration of exposure.
The study design excluded laboratory test results and utilized a single-center retrospective observational approach rather than a multicenter design.
Diseases were defined as requiring at least one inpatient record or two outpatient records within a year to improve diagnostic accuracy based on administrative codes.
Individual analyses for all medications were not performed because the analysis focused only on drugs with larger sample sizes.

Multiple comparisons across different antipsychotic agents were not explicitly adjusted, and medication adherence could not be directly assessed despite the application of an intent-to-treat approach.
The study provides the acquisition protocol and reliability statistics but omits software versions, calibration logs, and code, creating a gap that blocks verification of the reported variance.

While raw data and reliability statistics are provided, the specific code and parameter versions for the preprocessing step are absent, which is essential to determine if the reported AUC is an artifact of the cleaning pipeline.
Reproduction of the gait study is blocked by the absence of public scripts, leaving the preprocessing pipeline as an uncheckable black box.

The measurement paper for tremor quantification is blocked by missing acquisition parameters and an undocumented preprocessing pipeline, which prevents independent variance estimation and renders the 31-person healthy control group's baseline unreliable.

The validation study omits specific filter bands and motion correction algorithms, preventing verification of whether the 0.77 AUC is a valid physiological signal or an artifact of the cleaning pipeline.
The intervention trial lacks a pre-registered analysis plan for its primary endpoint, which creates a gap in the reproducibility of the reported effect size interpretation.

The cohort study relies on unadjusted diagnostic codes without strict enforcement of inpatient criteria, introducing a misclassification bias gap that compromises the reproducibility of the risk estimates.

The intervention trial is blocked from replication because the specific code for the anti-gravity treadmill calibration is missing, preventing verification of the force plate readings and raw gait data.
The validation study is blocked from replication because the preprocessing scripts and software versions are missing, making the reported 0.77 AUC impossible to re-run or verify.
The validation study's methods section fails to specify the motion correction algorithms and filter bands, leaving critical data processing parameters undefined for any attempt at reproduction.

Reproducing the claimed diagnostic signals requires a prospective trial with a fixed acquisition protocol and a validated control group, as the current reliance on retrospective data from opaque pipelines prevents independent verification of the results.

To prove the observed signals are biological rather than preprocessing artifacts, the methods must explicitly specify the exact motion correction and filtering steps used, a detail currently missing and necessary for replication.
The three studies fail to provide independent variance estimates, which blocks cross-validation and prevents the isolation of true signal from noise.

The uncorrected multiple comparisons in the current analyses inflate the Type I error rate, rendering the reported effects statistically unreliable without a prospective study with at least n = 100 per group to narrow the 95% confidence interval.

The preprocessing pipeline and acquisition parameters are unspecified in all three studies, meaning any future statistical analysis risks re-analyzing the same methodological artifacts rather than valid data.

The reported variance figures are currently unverifiable because the specific code and parameter settings are not available, preventing the distinction between true disease progression and transient artifacts.

OMT is thought to have a mean frequency range of 70-90 Hz in healthy adults. Previous research suggests OMT may be reduced in neurological diseases like Parkinson's Disease. Historically, OMT has been measured invasively in specialist laboratories using lengthy and expensive protocols. Developments now allow for OMT measurement quickly and non-invasively using hand-held technology (i.e., iTremor ONE). This pilot study aimed to examine the analytical and clinical validation of OMT measurement via the iTremor ONE in people with Parkinson's Disease (PwPD). 33 PwPD and 31 age matched healthy controls participated in this study. For analytical validation, 22 PwPD completed a test re-test reliability assessment of OMT measurement, assessed using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC). For clinical validation, OMT frequency in PwPD $(\mathrm{n}=33)$ was compared to controls. Correlations were explored with demographics and clinical scales. Additionally, 24 PwPD were tested 'OFF' (12hr withdrawal) and 'ON' their anti-Parkinson's (dopaminergic) medication to compare OMT response to a known intervention. The iTremor ONE demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (ICC>0.9) for measuring OMT frequency in PwPD. Mean OMT frequency was significantly lower in PwPD ( $63.78 \pm 4.82 \mathrm{~Hz}$ ) compared to controls $(69.44 \pm 6.47 \mathrm{~Hz}, \mathrm{p}<.001)$, with good discriminative ability (AUC 0.75-0.77). OMT frequency correlated with age in both groups and with specific motor features (speech, facial expression, gait) in PwPD. No significant differences in OMT frequency were observed between 'OFF' and 'ON' dopaminergic medication states. This is the first study to demonstrate that a non-invasive hand-held device can reliably measure OMT in PwPD and presents OMT analytical and clinical validation evidence. Further research is required to understand the neural mechanisms underpinning OMT in PwPD and the role it could play in clinical practice. ## Author summary Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the fastest growing neurological conditions globally, making early and accurate diagnosis increasingly important. Current assessment methods rely heavily on clinical observation, which can be subjective and may miss subtle early changes. We investigated whether a microscopic involuntary eye movement called ocular microtremor (OMT) could serve as an objective digital eye movement outcome measure for PD. Historically, measuring OMT required invasive, lengthy procedures where patients had their eyes held open for extended periods with probes placed directly on the eyeball, making them impractical for routine clinical use. We tested a new handheld device that measures OMT non-invasively for the first time in just three seconds using safe laser technology. We found the device gave highly reliable measurements and could distinguish between people with Parkinson's disease and healthy older adults with good accuracy. Interestingly, OMT related to specific symptoms like facial expression difficulties and walking problems but did not respond to PD medication. This suggests OMT may reflect brain chemistry beyond the dopamine system targeted by standard treatments, potentially involving other chemical messengers like acetylcholine. While larger studies are needed to confirm these findings, this quick, comfortable test could potentially complement existing tools for earlier diagnosis or disease monitoring in the condition.

Examination of eye movements is a key tool in neurological assessment as eye movements can be attributed to specific brain regions and their function [3-5]. Both voluntary and involuntary eye movements have been identified as promising biomarkers in neurological injury and disease and may provide a novel way to predict and track disease [6-10]. Current methodologies for the collection of eye movement data predominantly involve techniques which are highly subjective and often require lengthy protocols and invasive techniques [11]. As a result, there is a need for a quick, reliable, and non-invasive objective measurement tool to assess eye movements, including involuntary fixational eye movements.

As a result, there is a need for a quick, reliable, and non-invasive objective measurement tool to assess eye movements, including involuntary fixational eye movements. One such fixational eye movement is ocular microtremor (OMT), a subtle, microscopic eye movement that is present in everyone at all times [12]. OMT has gained some attention as a potential diagnostic and clinical tool in ophthalmology and neurology [13]. It is distinct from larger more noticeable eye movements, such as
saccades or smooth pursuit, and could potentially act as a more sensitive marker for neurological functioning, due to the complex neural mechanisms that underlie fixation [14]. It is an involuntary movement that has been reported to range from 70-150Hz (oscillates at 70-150 times per second [15]), in healthy subjects and cannot be seen by the naked eye, requiring specialised techniques to be quantified [16]. There is no gold standard technique for measurement of OMT, meaning that the application of OMT measurement protocols can vary as the microscopic movement is difficult to detect (e.g., video based eye-tracking systems don't possess the sensitivity required to detect OMT) [17]. Consequently, this limits generalisability and interpretation of underlying deficits [18]. Existing methods rely on invasive tools, such as the piezoelectric strain gauge technique, a probe is placed directly onto the eyeball, accelerometer fixed contact lenses, or eyelid fixed accelerometers which have several limitations (e.g., invasive nature, duration of protocols, need for specialist laboratory space and staff, and expense of equipment) [18]. Additionally, strain gauges or other techniques require the eyes to be anaesthetised [12,19-25], possess high interobserver variability, require a highly trained operator, and cause discomfort and eye dryness. It also relies on constant uninterrupted contact with the sclera meaning patients had their eye held open for up to 60minutes at a time, and there is an unknown loading effect of the probe, making validation of new techniques against this one undesirable [17,18,26]. Overall, invasive methods have limited application as a clinical tool for objective OMT as a biomarker. Given the previously demonstrated clinical utility, there is a need for a portable and non-invasive solution for measuring OMT. Further studies and advancements in OMT measurement techniques may lead to its potential integration into clinical practice for diagnostic and monitoring purposes in the future.

To date, there is little research on OMT, likely due to the lack of a quick, non-invasive measurement technique. As such, the underlying mechanisms of this subtle eye movement are not fully established. OMT has been postulated to link to brainstem activity [16,22,27]. Previous research has observed abnormal OMT characteristics in neurological conditions, such as Parkinson's Disease (PD) and Multiple Sclerosis [18,24,28,29]. It is thought that OMT originates from neural activity involving brainstem structures that excites the ocular motor nerves and causes the eye muscles to tremble [16,27,23]. However, the specific brainstem nuclei, pathways, and neurotransmitter systems involved remain uncertain.

However, the specific brainstem nuclei, pathways, and neurotransmitter systems involved remain uncertain. Previous work has shown altered OMT in PD [29]. PD is the fastest growing neurological disease in the world [30], with an estimated prevalence of 8.5 million globally [31]. While the hallmark motor features of PD result from dopaminergic cell loss in the substantia nigra pars compacta, pathological changes in PD affect brainstem nuclei early in the disease course [32]. The pathophysiology extends to multiple brainstem nuclei, including noradrenergic (locus coeruleus), serotonergic (raphe nuclei), and cholinergic (pedunculopontine nucleus) systems that have roles in various aspects of motor and non-motor function [33]. In PD, there are widespread neural mechanisms that underpin deficits in eye movement control. Given the hypothesized brainstem involvement in OMT generation and the documented brainstem pathology in PD, OMT abnormalities may reflect dysfunction in these neural systems. Despite evidence of altered OMT in PD using invasive measurement methods and the hypothesised link to brainstem pathology, no study has yet examined OMT using a non-invasive, portable technique in a clinical PD population. This represents a critical gap in the literature, as the absence of a non-invasive and practical measurement tool has prevented OMT from being evaluated as a clinically viable biomarker in PD.

Recent developments have led to the ability to record OMT with non-invasive and portable technology (i.e., The iTremor ONE, Head Diagnostics Ltd., Dublin, Ireland), which could allow relatively fast OMT measurement in various locations. This device uses laser technology to measure OMT and offers a high resolution non-invasive, compact, and portable technique for obtaining OMT data [34,35]. This method has been proven to be feasible and overcomes many of the current limitations associated with other more invasive techniques [36]. However, this new device has yet to undergo analytical and clinical validation to determine whether it is accurate, reliable, and sensitive to clinical groups of interest, such as PD.
